_comment: Per-work orientation descriptions shown in Browse Corpus and the Reader. Keyed by language, then by base work id (the .tess filename without language directory, extension, or .part suffix). Two or three plain sentences describing the TEXT itself: its contents, structure, and interest, with author and date kept brief. Every text import should add its entry here.

la.justin.epitome: An abridgement of the lost forty-four book universal history of Pompeius Trogus, made by Justin, probably in the second or third century AD. It narrates the empires of the Near East, Greece, and Macedon down to the rise of Rome, with special fullness on Alexander and his successors, and it is the main surviving narrative for much of Hellenistic history.
la.hyginus.fabulae: A handbook of roughly three hundred short mythological summaries compiled under the name of Hyginus, perhaps in the second century AD. Genealogies of gods and heroes, one-paragraph retellings of the great myth cycles, and catalogue chapters preserve the plots of many Greek myths and lost tragedies found nowhere else.
la.hyginus.astronomica: A handbook of the constellations attributed to the same Hyginus as the Fabulae. For each figure in the sky it tells the myth of how it was placed there, then describes its stars, drawing on the Greek catasterism tradition.
la.isidore.etymologiae: A twenty-book encyclopedia that approaches every subject through the origins of its words, covering grammar, rhetoric, law, medicine, the church, animals, geography, ships, buildings, food, and games. Compiled by Isidore, bishop of Seville (died 636), it preserves fragments of many lost ancient authors and became the most consulted reference work of the Middle Ages.
la.petrarch.africa: A Latin epic in nine books on Scipio Africanus and Rome's defeat of Hannibal in the Second Punic War, modeled on Virgil and drawing its history from Livy. Its set pieces include Scipio's dream, the love and death of Sophonisba, and Hannibal and Scipio meeting before Zama. Petrarch began it in 1338 and left it unfinished.
la.pomponius_mela.de_chorographia: The earliest surviving geography in Latin, written around AD 43. In three brisk books it tours the coasts of the known world, from the Strait of Gibraltar around the Mediterranean and back along the outer Ocean, mixing places and peoples with marvels.
la.varro.de_lingua_latina: A treatise on the Latin language by Varro (116 to 27 BC), of which books five through ten survive of twenty-five: three on where words come from and three on how they change form. It explains hundreds of Latin words for places, times, things, and actions, and it is a major source for archaic Latin and for Roman religious and legal antiquities.
la.varro.res_rusticae: A dialogue on farming in three books: field crops and the layout of the estate, cattle and sheep, and the profitable luxury trades of villa life such as aviaries, apiaries, and fishponds. Varro wrote it in 37 BC at the age of eighty, and with Cato's treatise it is our chief Roman work on agriculture.
la.velleius_paterculus.historiae_romanae: A compendium of Roman history in two books, running from the origins to AD 30 and moving quickly toward the writer's own times. It offers capsule sketches of Latin literary history found nowhere else and an admiring eyewitness portrait of Tiberius, under whom Velleius served as an officer.
la.frontinus.strategemata: A casebook of military stratagems arranged by type, on concealing plans, ambushes, sieges, discipline, and more, each chapter giving short historical examples of how commanders handled a recurring problem of war. Compiled by Frontinus, himself a senator and general, in the late first century AD.
la.frontinus.de_aquis: A treatise on the nine aqueducts of Rome: the history of each, its length and capacity, the laws governing the water supply, and the frauds uncovered when Frontinus became curator of the aqueducts in AD 97. A unique inside view of the administration of a great Roman public work.
la.sidonius.carmina: Twenty-four poems in the elaborate late antique manner: verse panegyrics of the emperors Avitus, Majorian, and Anthemius, and occasional pieces for friends on villas, baths, weddings, and books. Written by Sidonius Apollinaris in fifth-century Gaul before he became bishop of Clermont.
la.sidonius.epistulae: Nine books of literary letters modeled on Pliny, describing villas, dinner parties, libraries, church elections, and the Visigothic court while Roman rule in Gaul dissolved. They are the fullest picture we have of aristocratic life in the last generation of the western empire.
la.fronto.epistulae: The correspondence of the orator Fronto with Marcus Aurelius, his pupil and later emperor, together with letters to Lucius Verus, Antoninus Pius, and friends. The letters trade affection, criticism of each other's prose, and news of illness and family, and they were recovered from a palimpsest in 1815.
la.nemesianus.eclogae: Four pastoral poems in the line of Virgil and Calpurnius Siculus: shepherds mourn the dead poet Meliboeus, compete in song, and sing of love and of Pan and Bacchus. Written by Nemesianus of Carthage in the later third century AD.
la.nemesianus.cynegetica: A didactic poem on hunting: the breeding, rearing, and ailments of hounds, the choice of horses, and the huntsman's nets and gear, breaking off after 325 lines. Written by Nemesianus about AD 283.
la.nemesianus_pseudo.de_aucupio: Two short verse fragments on bird catching, one on taking partridge with an owl as decoy. Transmitted under the name of Nemesianus, though the attribution is doubted.
la.symmachus.epistulae: The collected letters of Symmachus, the leading pagan senator of late fourth-century Rome, published in ten books on the model of Pliny. Most are short notes of recommendation, courtesy, and senatorial business, and together they map the friendship networks of the late Roman aristocracy. Symmachus is best remembered for his plea to restore the Altar of Victory to the senate house.
la.abelard.historia_calamitatum: A long autobiographical letter, written about 1132, in which Abelard recounts his misfortunes: his rise as the most famous teacher of philosophy in Paris, the affair with Heloise and his castration, the condemnation of his book at Soissons, and his persecutions as monk and abbot. It frames the correspondence with Heloise that follows.
la.abelard.epistolae: The letters exchanged between Abelard and Heloise after the Historia calamitatum: her two letters of passionate reproach, his replies of consolation and counsel, and the letters of direction for the religious life of her convent of the Paraclete. Among the most famous correspondence of the Middle Ages.
la.gregorius_magnus.dialogi: Four books of dialogues on the miracles of the holy men of sixth-century Italy, told to the deacon Peter. The second book is a complete life of St. Benedict and the chief source for his biography, and the fourth treats the fate of the soul after death. Written by Pope Gregory the Great around 593.
la.gregorius_magnus.regula_pastoralis: A handbook on the office of bishop in four parts: who should undertake pastoral rule, the life the ruler ought to lead, how to adapt teaching to thirty-six contrasting pairs of characters, and the ruler's return to self-examination. Written by Gregory the Great soon after he became pope in 590, it shaped the medieval ideal of church leadership.
la.lactantius_placidus.in_statii_thebaida_c: An ancient line-by-line commentary on Statius's Thebaid, quoting the poem phrase by phrase and explaining its mythology, geography, and diction. Compiled perhaps in the fifth or sixth century AD under the name of Lactantius Placidus, it preserves a great deal of mythographic learning that would otherwise be lost.
la.aquinas.summa_theologiae_1: The First Part of Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologiae, written around 1265 to 1268: 119 questions on God, creation, the angels, and human nature, each divided into articles that argue objections, an answer, and replies. The famous five ways of proving God's existence stand near the opening, and the whole is woven from quotations of Scripture, Aristotle, Augustine, and Dionysius.
la.aquinas.hymni: The five eucharistic hymns composed for the feast of Corpus Christi in 1264 and attributed to Thomas Aquinas: Pange lingua, Lauda Sion, Sacris solemniis, Verbum supernum, and Adoro te devote. Tantum ergo, O salutaris hostia, and Panis angelicus are stanzas of these hymns, still sung today, and the openings deliberately echo the older hymns of Venantius Fortunatus.
la.erasmus.moriae_encomium: A mock oration in which Folly praises herself as indispensable to every human pursuit, moving from playful teasing of lovers and scholars to hard satire of monks, princes, and theologians. Erasmus wrote it in 1509 at Thomas More's house, punning on his friend's name, and the Latin is dense with allusions to Lucian, Horace, and the classical proverbs of his own Adagia. The text carries the standard 68 sections plus the prefatory letter to More.
la.erasmus.colloquia: Eighteen of the most famous of Erasmus's Colloquia familiaria, the short Latin dialogues published between 1518 and 1533: a shipwreck, a pilgrimage sent up as tourism, an abbot bested by a learned woman, Charon ferrying the war dead, an alchemist's con, and more. Written to teach conversational Latin, they became some of the sharpest social satire of the sixteenth century, banned and bestselling at once.
la.alan_de_insulis.anticlaudianus: Alan of Lille's philosophical epic, written around 1182 to 1183 in nine books with a prologue and epilogue. Nature convenes the Virtues to fashion a new perfect man, Prudence journeys through the heavens to fetch him a soul from God, and the finished man is armed for a climactic battle against Vice. Its title mocks Claudian's invective poem against Rufinus by proposing an opposite, and it strongly shaped later medieval allegory, including Chaucer and the Roman de la Rose.
la.alan_de_insulis.de_planctu_naturae: Alan of Lille's De Planctu Naturae, a dialogue in alternating prose and verse written around 1160 to 1170. Nature appears to the narrator lamenting that humanity alone among creatures breaks her laws, above all through unnatural vice, and the poem closes with Genius pronouncing excommunication on the offenders. A major source for later personification allegory, again including the Roman de la Rose.
la.bernard_silvestris.cosmographia: Bernard Silvestris's Cosmographia, also called De mundi universitate, a philosophical poem in alternating prose and verse written around 1147 and dedicated to Thierry of Chartres. In two books, Megacosmus and Microcosmus, Nature and divine Providence shape the universe out of primal matter and then fashion humanity as its image, drawing on Plato's Timaeus by way of Chalcidius. A founding text of twelfth century cosmological allegory and the Chartrian school.
la.cassiodorus.institutiones: Cassiodorus's Institutiones divinarum et saecularium litterarum, a two book guide to study written around 560 for the monks of his foundation at Vivarium. Book one surveys the books of Scripture and the church fathers with practical advice on copying and correcting manuscripts, and book two summarizes the seven liberal arts, from grammar through music. Cassiodorus, a former Roman praetorian prefect turned monastic founder who died around 580, helped set the curriculum that carried classical learning into the Middle Ages.
la.cassiodorus.variae: Cassiodorus's Variae, twelve books of official letters and government orders that he drafted, in his own name and in the names of Ostrogothic kings, across decades as a Roman administrator in Italy. They range from tax disputes and building repairs to appointments and diplomatic correspondence, composed in an elaborate rhetorical style, and together form the fullest surviving record of Roman civil administration under Ostrogothic rule. Cassiodorus assembled the collection around 537 as a showcase of his own official prose.
la.venantius_fortunatus.carmina: Venantius Fortunatus's Carmina, eleven books of occasional Latin poetry written after he settled in Merovingian Gaul around 566. The collection holds panegyrics to Frankish kings and bishops, personal poems to his patron Radegund and her convent at Poitiers, epitaphs, and hymns, including Vexilla regis and Pange lingua gloriosi, sung in church liturgy ever since. Fortunatus, who lived from about 530 to shortly after 600, is often called the last poet of late antiquity and the first of the Middle Ages.
la.venantius_fortunatus.vita_martini: Venantius Fortunatus's Vita Sancti Martini, a four book hexameter epic on the life and miracles of Martin of Tours, closely based on the prose Life and Dialogues of Sulpicius Severus. Fortunatus casts a saint's biography in the meter and diction of Virgilian epic and dedicates the poem to Gregory of Tours. It shows classical epic form carried forward to celebrate a Christian holy man.
la.walter_de_chatillon.alexandreis: Walter of Chatillon's Alexandreis, a ten book Latin epic on the life of Alexander the Great completed around 1180, closely following the ancient historian Quintus Curtius Rufus. Written in polished classicizing hexameters full of allusions to Virgil, Lucan, and Statius, it became a standard schoolroom text and one of the most admired Latin poems of the Middle Ages. Walter, who died around 1201 or 1202, taught at Chatillon-sur-Marne and Reims.
la.nigel_wireker.speculum_stultorum: Nigel Wireker's Speculum Stultorum, a twelfth-century Latin beast-fable satire in elegiac verse. Its hero is Burnellus, a donkey dissatisfied with the length of his tail, whose quest to grow a longer one becomes a vehicle for mocking the ambitions and hypocrisies of monks, clerics, and scholars of Wireker's day, and drifts into extended satire of university life and the corruption of the church courts. Wireker, a monk of Christ Church, Canterbury, died around 1198 to 1200.
la.johannes_hanville.architrenius: Johannes de Hauvilla's Architrenius, a Latin allegorical poem in hexameter verse written around 1184. It follows its grieving hero, whose name means arch-weeper, through personified vices and follies of the age, including the court of Venus, the poverty of student life in Paris, and the corruptions of ambition and greed, before a final meeting with the goddess Nature, who delivers a long philosophical discourse and gives him a wife named Moderation. Curtius cites the poem as an early source for the world-upside-down and locus amoenus topoi that recur across medieval and Renaissance literature.
la.carmina_burana.carmina_burana: A selection from the Carmina Burana, the large thirteenth-century manuscript collection of Latin poems by wandering scholars and clergy, copied at the Bavarian abbey of Benediktbeuern around 1230. This import covers the collection's serious and moral-satirical poems, including the Fortune-wheel lyrics, satires on clerical corruption, and the Archpoet's tavern confession, drawn from J. A. Schmeller's 1847 edition, the first to print the manuscript in full. The manuscript's love, drinking, and gambling songs are not included in this pass.
la.tiberianus.carmina: Four short poems and a few fragments attributed to Tiberianus, a fourth-century Roman senator who served as praetorian prefect of Gaul under Constantine. The best known is a twenty-line trochaic description of a locus amoenus, a shaded stream valley full of birdsong and flowers, cited by Curtius as an early landscape set piece that later poets kept imitating.
la.pentadius.carmina: Six short poems by Pentadius, a minor Latin poet of the third or fourth century known only from Riese's Anthologia Latina. The best known, De adventu veris, describes the arrival of spring through repeated end-of-line echoes, and it became a model for later medieval spring poems in the locus amoenus tradition.
la.prudentius.cathemerinon: The Liber Cathemerinon, twelve hymns by the Christian Latin poet Prudentius (c. 348 to after 405) for set hours of the day and the church calendar, including morning, evening, before meals, and hymns for the dead and for Christmas and Epiphany. Hymn 3, sung before sleep, describes Paradise as a garden watered by four rivers, a passage Curtius cites as a landmark instance of the locus amoenus topos carried into Christian poetry.
la.matthew_of_vendome.ars_versificatoria: A late twelfth-century Latin handbook on composing verse by Matthew of Vendome, mixing prose instruction with worked verse examples on describing people, places, and things, and on constructing arguments and transitions. Its long example description of an ideal landscape, with birdsong, a murmuring brook, and a warm breeze, became a widely copied model for the locus amoenus in medieval Latin poetry.
la.geoffrey_of_vinsauf.poetria_nova: Geoffrey of Vinsauf's Poetria Nova, a verse treatise on rhetoric and poetic composition written around 1208 to 1213 and dedicated to Pope Innocent III. Organized around the stages of invention, arrangement, and style, it was one of the most widely used medieval arts of poetry and quotes or imitates a wide range of classical and medieval verse to illustrate its rules.
la.geoffrey_of_vinsauf.documentum: Geoffrey of Vinsauf's Documentum de modo et arte dictandi et versificandi, a prose companion to his Poetria Nova covering the same ground on letter writing and verse composition in more schoolroom-manual form. It works through ways to begin a text, develop its body, and close it, with abundant classical quotation used as models.
la.eberhard_the_german.laborintus: The Laborintus, a Latin verse treatise on poetic and rhetorical training by Eberhardus Alemannus, known as Evrard the German, written in the early thirteenth century and framed as a complaint about the state of contemporary education. It is not to be confused with the Graecismus, a grammar textbook by a different author, Evrard of Bethune.
la.petrus_riga.de_ornatu_mundi: A short Latin poem in ninety elegiac couplets on the adornment of the created world, attributed to Peter Riga, the twelfth-century canon of Reims better known for his long verse Bible paraphrase the Aurora. Printed in Patrologia Latina under Hildebert of Lavardin's name, a long-standing misattribution, it surveys the beauty of the heavens, birds, flowers, and gems as signs of divine order.
la.caesar_pseudo.de_bello_africo: An account of Caesar's African campaign of 47 to 46 BC, from the landing at Hadrumetum to the victory at Thapsus and the death of Cato at Utica, written by an officer who served in it. It continues Caesar's own Civil War commentaries in another hand, plainer in style and close to the events, and is the fullest narrative of a single campaign in the Caesarian corpus after the Gallic War.
la.caesar_pseudo.de_bello_alexandrino: The war at Alexandria in 48 to 47 BC, with Caesar besieged in the palace quarter beside Cleopatra, followed by the campaigns in Illyricum, Spain and Pontus that ended at Zela. Written soon after the events by an author in Caesar's circle, perhaps Hirtius, to bridge Caesar's Civil War and the African war.
la.caesar_pseudo.de_bello_hispaniensi: The last campaign of the civil war, against Pompey's sons in Spain in 45 BC, ending at Munda. A short and rough narrative by a participant with no literary training, valued for the soldier's view of the fighting and for what its Latin shows of everyday usage.
la.vegetius.epitoma_rei_militaris: A handbook of Roman military practice in four books, written about AD 390 for an emperor, on the selection and training of recruits, the organisation of the legion, tactics in the field, and siegecraft and naval war. Compiled from earlier writers rather than from experience, it became the standard military text of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance.
la.grattius.cynegetica: A didactic poem on hunting in hexameters from the age of Augustus, treating the nets, spears, dogs and horses of the chase, with digressions on the origins of hunting and the diseases of dogs. About 540 lines survive. Ovid names Grattius among his contemporaries.
la.germanicus.aratea: A Latin rendering of Aratus' Phaenomena in hexameters by Germanicus, nephew and adopted son of Tiberius, made early in the first century AD. It describes the constellations and their myths, adapts Aratus to Roman astronomy and to Augustan poetry, and survives with fragments of a second part on weather signs.
la.solinus.collectanea_rerum_memorabilium: A compendium of geography and natural marvels from about the third century AD, moving region by region through the known world with its peoples, animals, stones and curiosities. Drawn largely from Pliny and Pomponius Mela, it was widely read through the Middle Ages and is the source of much later lore.
la.censorinus.de_die_natali: A birthday gift in the form of a learned treatise, addressed to a patron in AD 238. The first part treats human generation, the guardian spirit and the stages of life, the second the reckoning of time, calendars, eras and the date of the present year. It preserves much from lost writers on chronology and music.
la.obsequens.liber_de_prodigiis: A year by year list of prodigies from 190 to 11 BC, with lightning strikes, monstrous births, rains of stones, plagues and portents, each entry naming the consuls of the year and the expiation performed. Excerpted in the fourth century from Livy's history, it is the fullest surviving record of the Roman prodigy lists.
la.agius_of_corvey.epicedium_hathumodae: The Epicedium Hathumodae is a Carolingian Latin funerary lament in verse, attributed to Agius of Corvey, mourning Hathumoda, an abbess who died in the flower of her youth. Addressed to the grieving sisters of her community, the poem opens by recounting how the poet consoled them in person soon after her death and now casts that speech into verse at their request, adding further material so that they might reread his words of comfort. Across some 718 lines it praises the abbess's virtues and insists that grief, though natural, must be kept within the bounds of reason. Readers hunting parallels will find it a useful witness to the classical consolatio and epicedium traditions as refracted through Carolingian monastic verse.
la.agius_of_corvey.versus_computistici: Attributed to Agius of Corvey, the Versus Computistici is a Carolingian Latin didactic poem of 206 lines devoted to computus, the reckoning of the calendar. Its prologue praises number as the divinely granted fount of the arts and addresses a dedicatee named Rimbert, whose name is punningly glossed as 'renowned in number'; the verses then set out, for the benefit of learners rather than experts, the elements of time-reckoning — months, weeks, days and hours, epacts, concurrents, and the courses of sun, moon, and stars. The combination of computistical doctrine with a prefatory play on names and conventional gestures of command and obedience makes the poem a rewarding hunting ground for readers tracing textual parallels.
la.aimoin_of_saint_germain.carmen_de_transl: Carmen de Translatione Vincentii is a medieval Latin poem of sixty-five lines attributed to Aimoin of Saint Germain and assigned to the Carolingian era. It narrates how Audaldus, a priest-monk of Castellum who bears the honour of Aaron, journeys to Valentia in Spain, where his host Zacharias, won over by prayers and gifts of silver, discloses the resting place of Vincent the deacon and martyr; the relics are dug up by night amid miraculous signs and conveyed back to the fair cell of father Benedict at Castellum. The opening chronological computation, the nocturnal excavation, and the monks' joyful reception of the saint conform to the conventions of the relic-translation genre. The poem offers readers of intertexts Carolingian hagiographic diction, biblical allusion, and formulas shared with other accounts of the discovery and transfer of relics.
la.angilbert_carmina: A corpus of medieval Latin verse, 262 lines in all, by the Carolingian poet Angilbert, for which the source record supplies no meter. The opening poem is a welcoming address to Pippin, whose return from the Hesperian shores will fill his father Charles with joy, and it stages the longing of the brother Charles, the consoling report of Chlodowih, and a dream apparition of the absent brother promising speedy arrival, culminating in the poet's self-identification as 'Somni sed fructus Angilbertus ego.' The dense classical surface — Phoebus rising from the eastern stars, the waxing moon's horns, the rhetoric of delay and longing — makes the carmina fertile ground for tracing Virgilian and Ovidian echoes, court panegyric formulas, and the dream-vision motif in Carolingian court poetry.
la.anonymous.breviarius_de_hierosolyma: The Breviarius de Hierosolyma is a brief anonymous Latin prose itinerary of uncertain date that leads the reader through the holy places of Jerusalem, from the basilica of Constantine, Golgotha, and the church of the Holy Sepulchre to holy Sion, the house of Pilate, and the Mount of Olives. Each station is tied to a biblical event and to the relics preserved on the spot, including the True Cross, the Lance, the crown of thorns, and the chalice of the Last Supper. As a compact catalogue of Jerusalem's sacred topography, it serves as a useful parallel for readers tracing pilgrimage itineraries, relic traditions, and the scriptural geography of the city.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_aquilegia: The Carmen de Aquilegia is a brief anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, preserved in 75 lines. It commemorates Aquileia as a glorious and warlike metropolis of the Veneti, recounts the city's evangelisation through the apostle Mark and the martyr-bishop Hermagoras with his companions, and laments its ruin, first at the hands of Attila and later in the devastation wrought by the Avars, when priests, nobles, and virgins alike perished or were carried captive. The poem closes its opening movement by praising the Venetians as the enduring heirs of the faith once anchored at Aquileia, whose own citizens are rebuked for hardened wickedness. Readers pursuing intertexts will find here the Aquileian foundation and translation legends, the Venetian cult of Mark, and the medieval topos of a fallen metropolis whose ecclesiastical dignity passes elsewhere.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_conversione_saxonum: The Carmen de Conversione Saxonum is a short anonymous Latin poem of uncertain date, running to 75 lines, which commemorates the conversion of the Saxons under Charles, naming the ninth year of his reign. It opens with a providential survey of the world's ages, recounting creation, the fall, and Christ's redemptive victory over death and the underworld, before turning to the Saxons' former idolatry and bloody sacrifices and their reduction to Christianity by Carolingian arms. Its dense weave of biblical allusion and Christian Latin epic diction, together with its chronological and computistical framing, makes it rewarding material for readers tracing verbal and thematic parallels across patristic and early medieval verse.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_nynia_episcopo: A medieval Latin verse life of Bishop Ninian (Nynia), anonymous and of uncertain date, running to 504 lines. It opens with Christ's incarnation and the spread of grace through the world, then celebrates Ninian, named thus in his native tongue, his stupendous miracles, the crowds he won for Christ, and his voyage over the sea and across the Alps to be strengthened by the supreme pontiff. Its direct quotation of the Psalms and its high diction, which blends scriptural phrasing with classical poetic vocabulary, make it rewarding ground for readers tracing verbal and thematic echoes in hagiographic verse.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_temporum_ratione: A medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, transmitted anonymously, on the reckoning of time (computus). Across its 902 lines it treats the threefold division of time under divine authority, human institution, and natural custom, covering the Sabbath commandment, Olympiads, the length of the month, the circuits of the zodiac, and the fractional nomenclature — unciae, sextantes, semisses and their kin — by which hours and moments were subdivided. For readers of intertexts its interest lies in the versification of material more often transmitted in prose computistical handbooks, which makes the poem a useful witness for shared phrasing and doctrine across the medieval calendrical tradition.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_timone_comite: The Carmen de Timone Comite is an anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, surviving in 150 lines, which praises Count Timo, dispatched as the envoy of a king addressed in the second person to administer justice in the Norican lands. After a reference to a toilsome journey to Rome, the poet invokes his Thalia and sketches Timo as a restorer of neglected law, a scourge of thieves, robbers, and strife, and a lighten­er of the burdens of the innocent. The encomium is sustained by a chain of biblical exempla: David's severity towards the wicked and mildness to the good, Job's endurance and just kingship, the gentleness of Moses and Joshua, and Joseph's harshness towards his treacherous brothers. The poem thus offers a compact specimen of the medieval mirror-for-rulers mode and rewards readers tracing biblical commonplaces and the classical muse-invocation in Latin panegyric.
la.anonymus.karolus_magnus_et_leo_papa: Karolus Magnus et Leo Papa is an anonymous medieval Latin epic of 536 lines, of uncertain date, celebrating Charlemagne and his dealings with Pope Leo. The opening verses deploy the seafaring imagery of an epic prologue before moving into panegyric: Charlemagne, 'victor pius' and mightier than all kings in justice, is set against King David and the sun-god Phoebus, outshining the biblical king as the constant sun outshines the waning moon, while his rule joins piety, clemency, and divinely sanctioned discipline. Readers hunting textual parallels will find in the poem a Carolingian fusion of classical epic diction with biblical typology and the Latin panegyric tradition.
la.anonymus.laudes_mediolanensis_civitatis: Laudes Mediolanensis Civitatis is an anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, comprising 72 lines in praise of Milan. It celebrates the city's lofty situation, its twelve-foot walls, nine iron-bound gates, water supply, and splendid churches, then enumerates the saints buried there—Ambrose, Protasius, Gervase, Nazarius, Celsus, Benedict, and others—hailing Milan as queen of cities and metropolis toward which the bishops of Ausonia converge. As a specimen of the medieval urban encomium, it offers readers of intertexts parallels for topoi of city praise, relic catalogues, and the literary promotion of a see city through its sacred dead.
la.anonymus.versus_ad_ebonem_remensem: A medieval Latin poem of forty-six lines, of uncertain date and anonymous authorship, addressed to Ebbo, bishop of Reims, whom it praises through a dense string of honorific epithets. Its central section recounts the making of a Gospel book at Ebbo's command: the humble abbot and master Peter executed the commission, adorned the volume with gold within and ivory without, and dedicated it to the apostolic lord, while the poem enumerates the four Evangelists, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, whose writings the book contains. Christ figures throughout as the radiant physician whose gospel remedies heal the sick, and the closing lines ask that supplicants who seek his aid be granted the crown of everlasting peace. Readers of intertexts may find it a rich specimen of verse book-dedication, with the Evangelists likened to the quadriga of Christ and the medicine-of-Christ motif inviting parallels with inscriptional and exegetical traditions.
la.anonymus.versus_de_eversione_monasterii_: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of 78 lines, of uncertain date, bearing the title Versus de Eversione Monasterii Glonnensis and lamenting the burning of the monastery of Glonn and its basilica of Saint Florentius by a cruel, brutish Britannic people. The verses open with an Orphic invocation to the Thracian lyre and then recount the foundation of the church by the mighty King Charles, who endowed it with fertile lands and a vessel of the Lord's Supper famed for restoring the sick, and its continued favour under his son Louis. On Louis's death the kingdom is partitioned four ways, discord spreads among the warring sons, and a once-poor husbandman named Nemenoius, enriched by a buried treasure, rises through deceit to take up arms against Charles. The poem offers readers of intertexts a classicizing proem alongside hagiographic and dynastic narrative, including an early account of a wonder-working eucharistic vessel.
la.augustine.locutiones_in_heptateuchum: The Locutiones in Heptateuchum is a short Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, a philological and theological commentary of some 737 lines on the first seven books of the Bible. It proceeds phrase by phrase through Genesis and the following books, explaining Latin renderings that look awkward or ambiguous as products of Hebrew and Greek idiom, citing the Greek versions and variant Latin readings, and noting habitual scriptural formulas such as 'et factum est'. For readers of intertexts, the work is valuable because it records the wording of the Latin Bible Augustine knew, his awareness of translation problems behind familiar verses, and the interpretive habits that inform his own scriptural allusions elsewhere.
la.ausonius.epistularum: A collection of prose epistles by the Late Antique author Ausonius, the Epistularum runs to some 1,623 lines and assembles short letters of friendship, thanks, and literary encouragement. The correspondence couples everyday courtesies—praise of a correspondent's writings, urging further composition, reflections on whether a published poem can be kept private—with polished Ciceronian diction, as in the opening letter's 'Tulliano melle' and its sententia that 'oratio publicata res libera est'. Readers hunting intertexts will find a late witness to the vocabulary and rhythm of classical epistolography, along with exempla drawn from the Roman stage (Roscius, Ambivius) and aphorisms readily reused across Latin prose.
la.ausonius.griphus_ternarii_numeri: The Griphus ternarii numeri, a riddling poem of some ninety lyric lines attributed to Ausonius in the late antique corpus, is an extended encomium of the number three, cast as a catalogue of triads drawn from mythology, ritual, and natural lore. Its verses enumerate such triplets as Nestor's nine-times-nine generations, the triform Hecate, the three Charites and Fates, and the Sphinx's riddle of two feet, four feet, and three, moving from sacred law to learned paradox. For readers of intertexts, the poem offers a dense web of allusions to Greek and Roman myth and a rare specimen of the numerical griphus as a literary form, making it a productive source for tracing triadic formulas and catalogue techniques in later verse.
la.ausonius.praefatiunculae: The Praefatiunculae are a brief collection of prefaces, sixty-seven lines in lyric verse, by Ausonius, a Latin poet of the late antique period. The opening poem is largely autobiographical, tracing the poet's origins from a physician father at Burdigala and kin among the Vasates, the Haedui, and the Tarbelli, through his career as grammarian and rhetor, his appointment to teach the imperial family, and his ascent to the quaestorship, the prefecture of Gaul, Libya, and Latium, and the consulship; it closes by recruiting the reader as patron of his poems. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact exercise in poetic self-fashioning, dense with learned reference to figures such as Aemilius, Scaurus, the Berytian Probus, Alcides, the Aeacides, and Chiron, and a useful parallel for the Latin tradition of the autobiographical preface.
la.ausonius.precationes: The Precationes, a 69-line lyric prayer by the late-antique poet Ausonius, opens with the refrain 'Iane, veni' and invokes Janus and the sun over the new consular year in which Ausonius himself holds the fasces. The poem petitions for favorable seasons and auspicious stars, then hails victories over Franks, Suebi, Sauromatae, Huns, Getae, and Alani, and the Caesar who is to succeed to Ausonius's consulship. A reader hunting parallels will find here a late-antique reworking of Roman New Year prayer, lyric refrain technique, and the seasonal and astrological catalogs familiar from Horatian and Ovidian practice.
la.ausonius.versus_paschales_pro_augusto_di: A brief Latin poem of thirty-one lines, the Versus Paschales pro Augusto Dicti (Easter verses spoken on behalf of the emperor) is attributed to Ausonius and belongs to the Christian verse of late antiquity. Opening on the paschal fast, the poem unfolds as a prayer to God the Father, maker of earth, sea, air, Tartarus, and the starry heaven, who pities deceived Adam and sends his Son, 'true from true, living from living origin,' to restore immortality through baptism and the single-authored threefold faith. It then turns to praise an Augustus who shares an undivided sovereignty with brother and son alike, 'father and begetter of two Augusti,' and closes by commending the earthly rulers to Christ before the eternal Father. Readers of intertexts will find here a characteristic fusion of imperial panegyric with Biblical diction on the Fall, the Trinity, and baptism, set within classically colored cosmic imagery.
la.avitus_of_vienne.de_spiritalis_historiae: The De spiritalis historiae gestis of Avitus of Vienne is a Late Antique Latin epic in hexameter verse, running to some 2,550 lines and divided into five books. Opening with a prologue on the origin of human toil, sin, and mortality and on Christ's redemptive payment, the poem proceeds into a grand account of the creation of the world, its lights, and its living kinds. Its fusion of classical epic diction with the Genesis narrative makes the work a rich source of parallels for readers tracing how Virgilian language and style were turned to biblical story in late Latin poetry. The edition followed is Migne's 1847 Patrologia Latina text, presented in classical Latin orthography.
la.candidus_of_fulda.epitaphia_aegili: Attributed to Candidus of Fulda, a short Carolingian Latin composition of nineteen lines preserving two epitaphs for Eigil, abbot of Fulda. The first, a twelve-line titulus, summons the passing reader to read the inscription and recounts the abbot's deeds — his happy governance of the monastery, his translation of a martyr's relics with the bishop, the dedication of two churches — closing with a signature by his successor Hrabanus, who calls himself unworthy. The second gives Eigil a speaking voice from the tomb: he rests in the small sepulchre he built while alive and awaits the Lord who will loose the bonds of death and raise him. Readers hunting intertexts will find here the classic address to the passerby, the speaking-deceased inscription, and stock formulas of Carolingian memorial verse that reach back to late antique epitaph and epigram.
la.cato_the_elder.de_agricultura: De Agricultura is a Latin prose treatise on estate management by Cato the Elder, composed during the Roman Republic. Opening with a defense of farming against trade and moneylending, it sets out practical precepts for buying and inspecting a farm, ranking soils and their best uses, supervising the vilicus and the slave familia, and cultivating vines, olives, and other crops, with attention to equipment, accounts, and the seasonal round of labor. Written in terse early Latin prose, the work preserves formulaic instructions and moral themes that later Roman agricultural and didactic writers drew upon, making it a key point of departure for tracing agrarian intertexts.
la.claudian.carmina_minora: The Carmina Minora assembles the shorter poems of Claudian, a Latin poet of Late Antiquity writing in hexameter and largely in the panegyric mode. The opening lines celebrate the general Stilicho, playing on his marriage ties to the imperial house ('Stilicho socer est, pater est Stilicho'), while other passages build mythological set pieces that set contemporary subjects against Geryon's triple-bodied cattle, the bulls of Clitumnus, and the monsters of Crete. Spanning some 1,867 lines as a single collection, the work offers readers of intertexts a compact quarry of mythological exempla, Castalian and Apollonian diction, and encomiastic invention through which late antique court poetry reworked classical tradition.
la.claudian.de_bello_gothico: A Latin panegyric in 665 hexameter lines by the late antique poet Claudian, De Bello Gothico celebrates the campaigns of Stilicho against the Goths. Its prologue announces the poet's return to song after an absence of years and weighs the hazards of praising Stilicho before a public audience, while the narrative opens with an extended comparison between the general and Tiphys, who steered the Argo through the clashing Symplegades. Dense with epic and mythological allusion in the service of contemporary politics, the poem offers fertile ground for tracing how late antique panegyric reworks heroic and voyage imagery from earlier Latin and Greek tradition.
la.claudian.in_consulatum_olybrii_et_probin: A Late Antique Latin panegyric in hexameters by Claudian, running to 279 lines, composed in honour of the joint consulship of Olybrius and Probinus. The poem opens with a cosmological address to the sun and the turning of the consular year, then praises a noble lineage in which the fasces descend unbroken from ancestor to heir, before celebrating the deeds and virtues of the two consuls in turn. For readers hunting textual parallels it offers a compact specimen of Late Antique encomium, dense with epic diction, celestial similes, and echoes of Augustan and imperial Latin verse.
la.claudian.in_eutropium: In Eutropium is a two-book Latin poem in hexameters by the Late Antique poet Claudian, totalling 1191 lines and catalogued as panegyric though in substance a sustained invective against the eunuch consul Eutropius. The first book opens with a catalogue of prodigies attending the consulship — wolf-born offspring, talking cattle, twin suns and clashing moons — and an appeal to the Sibylline verses and Etruscan haruspicy, before a speech of Fortune laments the consul's servile origins, his degraded past, and his corruption of public life. For readers of intertexts, the poem offers dense Virgilian and Ovidian texture and a showpiece Late Antique deployment of the Roman traditions of prodigy, Sibylline consultation, and divine personification.
la.claudian.panegyricus_de_sexto_consulatu_: A late antique Latin panegyric in hexameters by Claudian, running to 686 lines, celebrating the sixth consulship of the emperor Honorius. The poem opens with a nocturnal dream vision in which the poet's devotion to the Muses bears his song before the very throne of Jupiter, recounting the defeat of Enceladus and Typhoeus and the rewards of the Phlegraean campaign, until Honorius himself appears as 'orbis apex aequatus Olympo' and the dream proves true. The praise then unfolds through the temple owed to Fortune, the auguries of the auspicious year, and a fusion of civic and martial imagery — consular robes, the Campus Martius, the joining of Quirinus to the soldiery — that presents the emperor's majesty as native, cosmic, and divinely sanctioned. Its dream proem, mythological exempla, and dense epic diction make the work a productive source of parallels for classical epic language and panegyrical convention.
la.commodian.instructiones: The Instructiones of Commodian, a theological work of the later Imperial period in Latin, runs to 1,257 lines across two books. Its opening preface announces the aim of showing the errant the way to eternal life and recounts the author's own turn from pagan observance after reading the law. The instruction that follows urges abandonment of vain idols, rehearsing the giving of the law through Moses, the fall of the angels and the birth of the giants, and polemic against deities such as Saturn. Readers hunting biblical paraphrase, apologetic commonplaces, and anti-pagan topoi in later Imperial Latin Christian literature will find dense material for parallel-hunting.
la.dicuil.versus: A short Carolingian Latin poem of nineteen lines ascribed to Dicuil, who names himself within the verses and addresses the son begotten of Charles together with Louis, Charles's successor, placing the piece in the circle of the Carolingian court. The poet presents his work as playful 'argumenta' composed in praise and riddling fashion, taking the calendar as its theme from the month of April onward, and closes with a humble offering likened to the widow's two mites of the Gospels. Its internal computation of years points to a composition in 814, at the transition from Charlemagne's reign to that of Louis the Pious. The poem offers useful parallels for intertextual study of Carolingian occasional verse, calendrical riddling, and scriptural allusion in courtly panegyric.
la.ermoldus_nigellus.carminum_appendix: A brief appendix of 52 hexameter lines, classed with epic verse, attached to the Carmina of the Carolingian poet Ermoldus Nigellus. The opening sequence addresses a pipe and a boy performer charged with singing for King Pippin, pairing catalogue lines on exotic tribute and wares — Indian ivory, Sabean incense, Jordan balsam, Attic agates, Arabian gold — with recurring refrains urging the child to gather heavenly gifts and learn what Sophia teaches. A closing section turns commemorative and autobiographical, recording how Louis was crowned by Pope Stephen with Bishop Ebbo present, foundations of a place renewed, and the poet's own rearing on the Rhine, Loire and Seine. Readers of intertexts will note the explicit signposting of Virgil's Muse and Cato's sayings alongside the psalms, and the refrain-based structure, which makes the piece a compact showcase of Carolingian classical and biblical synthesis.
la.giovanni_aurelio_augurelli.chrysopoeia: Chrysopoeia ('gold-making') is a Latin didactic poem in four books, totalling 2,056 lines, by the Renaissance author Giovanni Aurelio Augurelli, on the alchemical art of producing gold. The proem claims that no poet before him had treated the gold-bearing art in verse, addresses a patron imagined as sent from heaven to relieve a weary world and to usher in a golden age of peace, and defends the poem's use of pagan deity-names such as Sol, Luna and Vulcan as conventional cover for alchemical materials and processes. For readers of intertexts, the poem offers a striking example of the classical didactic tradition — invocation of the Muses, patronal dedication, mythological allegory — refashioned for Renaissance alchemy, and it stands as a locus for tracing how ancient metallurgical and mythological vocabulary passed into early modern technical verse.
la.godescalcus_saxus.carminum_appendix: Carminum Appendix is a short collection of medieval Latin devotional verse (91 lines) attributed to Godescalcus Saxus and assigned to the Carolingian era. The opening poem is a penitential prayer that addresses Christ as the light of the speaker's darkness and pleads for deliverance from sin and a heart that loves God, before passing into hymnic praise of Christ as the eternal Word through whom the heavens, stars, seas, and earth were made. For readers hunting textual parallels, the work's compact scope and its pairing of penitential supplication with a creation hymn make it a convenient touchpoint for comparison with Carolingian devotional and hymnic verse.
la.hegesippus_pseudo.de_excidio_hierosolymi: A late antique Latin prose history of uncertain date attributed to Hegesippus (hence Pseudo-Hegesippus), the De Excidio Hierosolymitano recounts Jewish history from the Maccabean revolt down to the Roman capture of Jerusalem and the burning of the temple under Titus. Its prologue presents the work as a continuation of sacred history in historiographical style and openly reworks Josephus, whom the author faults for partiality toward the Jews and for failing to grasp the divine cause of their calamities. Readers hunting intertexts will find here a dense Christian Latin recasting of Josephus interwoven with biblical diction and the idiom of classical historiography, making the work a key witness to the Latin transmission of the Jerusalem narrative.
la.hibernicus_exul.carmina: The Carmina attributed to Hibernicus Exul ('the Irish exile'), a poet of the Carolingian period, are preserved in E. Dümmler's 1881 edition and total 594 lines of Latin verse. The collection opens with a prayer asking God to strengthen, prolong, and crown the life of Caesar Karolus — Charlemagne — whose peace, victories, and future heavenly reward it celebrates, and then turns to a covering note and an epistolary poem addressed to Gundrada, a girl praised for beauty and virtue, which unfolds into a vision of the world's magnates honouring their king with silver, gold, gems, purple, and horses. The verse's stated artlessness ('versibus incomptis' offered 'summo mentis amore'), its biblical and liturgical cadences, and its formulas of Christian rulership panegyric make the corpus a rewarding witness for readers tracing shared diction and topoi among the Latin poets who wrote for and about Charlemagne.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.ad_leonem_papa: Ad Leonem Papam is a short Latin theological work of 204 lines transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers; the attribution is pseudepigraphic, and the real author and date are uncertain, though the piece belongs to the later imperial period. As the title indicates, it is framed as an address to a pope Leo, whose request the speaker professes to have obeyed before embarking on a hymnic celebration of God the Father as the unbegotten source of all things. The opening lines, cast in epic-style verse, move from a formal dedication to an account of creation, in which the pre-existent deity kindles light out of chaos and orders the elements, seed, creatures, and souls of the infant world. Readers of intertexts may value the work as an example of Genesis narrative fused with the cosmogonic vocabulary and motifs of classical Latin epic.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.hymni: A short Latin collection of Christian hymns transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers, though the ascription is conventional and the authorship uncertain. The work, placed in the Later Imperial period and classed as theology, opens with a morning hymn hailing Christ as the true light of the world, outshining the lesser luminary that merely announces the coming day, and continues with penitential pieces in which the sinner, weighed down by the burden of sin, implores the Redeemer for pardon. Despite the prose classification in the source record, the hymns display the rhythmic, stanza-like character of early Latin Christian song, with dense biblical diction throughout. Readers hunting intertexts will find early formulations of the Christ-as-light topos and liturgical phrasing that resonate across patristic writing and later hymnody.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_mysterio_missae: A medieval Latin poem of 788 lines, De Mysterio Missae is attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin, whose speaker names himself in the opening lines as Hildebert of Le Mans (Cenomanus). The work begins with a riddling apology in which the poet pleads indulgence for his faults, styles himself Davus and dares the reader to be Oedipus, the successive lines being linked by the repetition of their closing words. The body of the poem expounds the mystery of the Mass: Christ the true host offered once for the many, the priest's ministry at the altar of temple and cross, and the fulfilment of the old law's figures in the true sacrifice. For readers of intertexts, its dense weave of scriptural and liturgical phrasing and its typological treatment of sacrificial imagery make it a rewarding witness to medieval Latin diction on the Eucharist.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_querimonia_et_c: A medieval Latin poem of 154 lines, of uncertain date and attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin, the De Querimonia et Conflictu Carnis et Spiritus stages the contest between flesh and spirit as a lament answered by consolation. The opening complaint gives voice to a soul figured as a frail and crumbling house, held in servile condition, and as a woman wed to Christ whose early devotion to her heavenly bridegroom is betrayed through the wiles of an adulterer who flatters her with delights, riches, and name. Yearning for release from a bitter covenant, she asks for a dwelling where she may live free, and a comforting voice replies that her desire will be granted. The poem's allegory of the soul as the spouse of Christ led astray, together with its imagery of house, prison, bridal chamber, and adulterer, makes it a useful witness for readers tracing the body-and-soul debate and the personified complaint tradition in medieval moral verse.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.in_primum_caput_ec: In Primum Caput Ecclesiastes is a medieval Latin poem of 171 lines by Hildebert of Lavardin, a versified commentary on the opening chapter of Ecclesiastes. The poem takes successive clauses of the Vulgate—'Vanitas vanitatum, dixit Ecclesiastes', 'generatio praeterit, et generatio advenit', 'oritur sol et occidit'—as lemmata and expounds each in verse. Its themes run from the vanity of all created things and the restless mutability of nature through the passing of generation after generation and death's scattering of amassed wealth to the final fire in which the four elements perish so that a purified earth may endure. Readers of intertexts will find it a compact witness to the medieval currency of the Vanitas vanitatum formula and of the Preacher's images of the sun's circuit and fleeting generations, stock material on which later writers repeatedly drew.
la.hrabanus.carmen_evangeliorum: A brief Latin poem attributed to the Carolingian author Hrabanus (Hrabanus Maurus), of uncertain exact date, on the four Evangelists and their symbolism. Its thirty-seven lines enumerate Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, the regions of their preaching (Judaea, Egypt, Achaia, Asia), and the tetramorphic figures of man, ox, lion, and eagle, before offering a tropological reading of these mystical forms and closing on the concord of the four Gospels. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact Carolingian witness to the evangelist iconography and allegorical exegesis inherited from patristic tradition.
la.hrabanus.carmina: A Carolingian Latin verse collection of 3,237 lines transmitted under the name of Hrabanus. The opening poem, a dedicatory prayer to a saintly bishop, recounts how a Frankish boy was sent by his abbot, rector of the Fulda fold, from the forest of Bochonia to learn at the saint's church the art of metre and sacred scripture, and how, once thirty years had passed ('sex lustra'), he offered a book in praise of Christ, instilled with typological numbers and tropological figures to display the gifts of God and the glory of Christ's passion foretold by prophets and by the letter of the law. Its self-conscious account of figured and typological verse-making, together with dense biblical diction throughout the collection, makes it rewarding terrain for readers tracing Carolingian engagement with earlier poetic and scriptural models.
la.hrabanus.laudes_crucis: A Latin poem in praise of the cross by the Carolingian writer Hrabanus, Laudes Crucis runs to some 1,110 lines of medieval devotional verse. Its proem invokes the Muse and, in a humility topos, presents the speaker as a poor and needy servant whose slight offering is justified by the biblical examples of the widow's mite and the gifts brought to the temple under the old law. The poem then exalts the cross as the sacred trophy of the crucified king, full of divinity and apt for every good. Readers tracing intertexts may find it valuable as an instance of Carolingian cross-veneration poetry that fuses classical invocation conventions with scriptural exempla and allegorical reflection on the Passion.
la.johannes_hymonides.versiculi_de_cena_cyp: A Carolingian Latin poem of 383 lines attributed to Johannes Hymonides, the Versiculi de Cena Cypriani offers a versified treatment of the Cena Cypriani, the allegorical banquet tale that its prologue associates with Cyprian of Carthage. The poem frames itself as a learned jest ('satira') for the pope's Easter festivities and for the banquet of the emperor Charles, and then unfolds a wedding feast at Cana hosted by King Iohel, at which Adam, Eve, Cain, Abel, Noah, the apostles, and a long train of biblical figures take their seats, each marked out by an action drawn from scripture. Its dense chain of scriptural reminiscences and its recasting of a prose banqueting catalogue into verse make it a rewarding witness for readers tracing the medieval Cena Cypriani tradition and the play of biblical intertext at the Carolingian court.
la.john_scotus_eriugena.carmina: A collection of medieval Latin verse attributed to John Scotus Eriugena, of Carolingian date, comprising some 845 lines. The opening poem is programmatic, setting the pagan epic tradition—Homer's songs of Hellas and Troy and Virgil's Romulean progeny—against Christian hymnody on Christ's Passion, the wood of the cross, the two thieves, and the darkness and earthquake at the Crucifixion. Classical allusion and biblical paraphrase are interwoven throughout, and the explicit staging of Homer and Virgil as foils makes the collection valuable for tracing how Carolingian Latin poets refashioned inherited classical models for Christian themes.
la.juvencus.historia_evangelica: The Historia Evangelica of Juvencus, a Latin poem of the later imperial period, casts the narrative of the Gospels into four books of hexameter verse in the manner of classical epic. Opening with the annunciation of John the Baptist to the priest Zacharias, the poem retells the gospel story in elevated epic diction across 3,182 lines. It offers readers of intertexts a central example of biblical epic, in which the conventions of Latin hexameter poetry are turned to scriptural material, and a rich source of verbal and stylistic parallels between classical and Christian traditions.
la.lactantius.carmen_de_passione_domini: The Carmen de Passione Domini is a short Late Antique Latin poem of eighty lines attributed to Lactantius. Christ himself is the speaker, addressing a passer-by at the doors of a temple and recounting the Incarnation, his birth in a Judaeaean manger, the flight from Herod into Egypt, a ministry of teaching and miracles pursued in poverty, and finally the betrayal, trial before Pilate, and crucifixion. By recasting the Gospel Passion narrative in the diction and posture of classical epic, the poem offers intertext-seeking readers a compact case study in how Christian Latin verse absorbs and repurposes earlier poetic language.
la.lactantius.de_ave_phoenice: A Late Antique Latin poem on the phoenix, attributed to Lactantius and edited from Samuel Brandt's 1897 Vienna edition of the Opera omnia. Its 170 lines portray an idyllic eastern paradise, a grove sacred to the Sun that escaped the flames of Phaethon and the flood of Deucalion and knows neither disease, old age, nor death, where the solitary phoenix dwells as the servant of Phoebus and renews its life through its own death. The poem's fusion of classical mythological allusion with a theological vision of rebirth made it a key vehicle for resurrection and paradise imagery, and its dense engagement with earlier phoenix and Golden Age traditions rewards readers hunting verbal and thematic parallels in late antique verse.
la.lios_monocus.libellus_sacerdotalis: A Latin didactic poem of 565 lines from the Carolingian period, the Libellus Sacerdotalis is attributed to an author given as Lios Monocus. The work opens with a prayer to Christ for eloquence before turning to exhortations addressed to priests, urging them to cultivate fitting conduct and to resist the devil, who is depicted tempting a young man with seductive arguments that divine mercy will excuse persistent sin. Its stark contrast of infernal darkness with the bliss of the saints in paradise, together with its staging of demonic rhetoric and advice to clergy, makes it relevant to readers tracing temptation scenes and admonitory clerical verse in the medieval Latin tradition.
la.lupus_servatus.versus: A brief Latin poem of twenty-seven lines attributed to Lupus Servatus, a Carolingian author, and addressed to an Evrardus. The verses form a dedication for a law book that Evrardus had caused to be written, cataloguing the peoples depicted in its pictures — the Salian Franks, Ripuarians, Lombards, Alamanni, and Bavarians — together with their laws, and acclaiming the figures of Carolingian rulers from Charles and Pippin to the emperor Louis and Lothar. The closing lines carry an authorial signature ('infimus ecce Lupus'), a promise of worthier song should life be spared, and a trinitarian blessing on the dedicatee. For readers hunting intertexts, the poem offers a compact instance of Carolingian verse attached to the transmission of the early medieval law codes, its diction echoing the language of legal compilation and book presentation.
la.macrobius.fragment: A brief Latin prose fragment, twelve lines in all, transmitted under the name of Macrobius, a Late Antique author. Its lines sketch a satirical scene of dissolute Roman public life: men gamble, drench themselves in perfume, and drain every amphora on the way to the comitium, where a drowsy judge demands documents he can scarcely read, before the deliberation collapses into a banquet catalogue of mulsum mixed with Greek wine, a fat thrush, a fine fish, and a wolf caught between two bridges. The comic diction and stock episodes — the drunken juror, the parade of dishes — echo the manner of earlier Latin satire and comedy, giving readers of intertexts a compact locus for verbal parallels within Roman satiric writing.
la.macrobius.saturnalia: The Saturnalia, a late-antique Latin prose work in seven books by Macrobius (Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius), casts its erudition as a series of banquets held during the Saturnalian festival at the house of Vettius Praetextatus, where Symmachus, Albinus, Servius, Eusebius the rhetorician, and other Roman notables discuss antiquities, religion, grammar, literature, and philosophy. The prefatory letter to the author's son Eustachius presents the work as a digest of wide Greek and Latin reading, in which material from earlier authors, often in their very words, is reordered into an organic whole, as bees gather and transform the nectar of many flowers. Its dense texture of quotation and adaptation makes the dialogue a prime hunting ground for textual parallels and for the transmission of classical learning in late antiquity.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.petitorium_quo_abs: A Latin prose petition (petitorium) by Magnus Felix Ennodius, a writer of the late antique period, in which the speaker formally manumits his slave Gerontius and requests his admission to the ecclesiastical college of Rome. The piece opens with a meditation on divine justice, the rewards of the faithful, and the consolation grace affords to those bound by earthly cares, then praises Gerontius' faith, chastity, and freeborn character before restoring his liberty and asking that he be released from every obligation in the church's records, with his property secured without diminution. Readers of intertexts may find value in the way the document fuses late Roman legal formulae of manumission with Christian vocabulary of grace, judgment, and reward, framing freedom as both a judicial act and a return of the soul to its divine origin.
la.ovid.heroides: The Heroides, an Augustan collection of verse epistles in elegiac couplets by Ovid, presents fictional letters from heroines of myth — beginning with Penelope writing to the still-absent Ulysses — to their absent or faithless lovers and husbands. Each letter compresses an entire epic or tragic storyline into the voice of female complaint, rewriting Homer and the tragic tradition from the perspective of the women left behind. For readers of intertexts the collection is central both as an intricate reworking of earlier Greek and Roman literature and as a model repeatedly imitated, answered, and reworked by later Latin, medieval, and Renaissance writers.
la.ovid.remedia_amoris: Ovid's Remedia Amoris, an Augustan elegy of 814 lines in elegiac couplets, presents itself as the therapeutic counterpart to the Ars amatoria: having taught how love is acquired, the poet now offers remedies to lovers whom unhappy passion drives to desperation. The opening dialogue has Cupid read the book's title and protest, while the speaker defends his earlier instruction and promises aid to those suffering under the rule of cruel girls, even invoking lovers driven to the brink of suicide. For readers of intertexts, its running engagement with Ovid's own amatory poetry and its dense texture of mythological exempla make it a central site for tracing allusion within Roman elegy.
la.paschasius_radbertus.carmina: A brief Carolingian Latin verse collection of 235 lines ascribed to Paschasius Radbertus and transmitted without book division. The opening and longest piece is an elaborate funerary lament (planctus) for a departed 'father', urging every rank — men, boys, girls, clerics, and rustics speaking Roman and Latin alike — to weep, strew flowers, raise a tomb, and add song to it, while alternating voices deliver divine poems and prayers for the old man's pardon and reception into paradise. Its diction fuses biblical and liturgical language with the rhetoric of classical lament and epitaph, and a versicle introduced by 'cecinit quam maximus ille' embeds quotation of earlier verse within the mourning. For readers of intertexts the poem offers evidence for Carolingian reworking of the planctus and consolatio traditions and for the citation of prior poetry inside an elegiac frame.
la.paulinus_of_aquileia.versus_de_destructi: A 92-line Carolingian Latin poem ascribed to Paulinus of Aquileia, the Versus de Destructione Aquilegiae is a lament for the destruction of Aquileia, once the wealthy and illustrious metropolitan city of Venetia, resplendent with clergy and churches dedicated to Christ. The poem casts the catastrophe as divine punishment: the city's pride, swollen amid its delights, provoked the wrath of the eternal judge, who raised up a cruel people from the east under Attila, depicted as a savage, godless lion, whose vast host besieged, burned, and razed the city, sparing neither age nor sex and driving the survivors into captivity. Readers hunting parallels will find here a Carolingian instance of the planctus over a fallen city, with the augural omen of birds nesting in the towers and the recurrent medieval motif of civic superbia drawing down vengeance in the enduring tradition of Attila's sack of Aquileia.
la.paulinus_of_pella.eucharisticus: The Eucharisticus (or Eucharisticon) of Paulinus of Pella is a Late Antique Latin Christian poem of thanksgiving in which an aged aristocrat recounts his whole life as a sequence of divine gifts, prefaced by a prose introduction explaining his purpose. The verse narrative recalls his birth near Thessalonica, his childhood and education at Bordeaux, a worldly youth of wealth and leisure, the loss of family and property during the Gothic and Alanic devastations of Gaul, and a poor old age spent at Massilia (Marseilles), all offered to Christ in gratitude. Readers of intertexts will find it valuable both as an early experiment in Christianized autobiography and for its self-conscious engagement with the classical authors—Homer and Virgil among them—whom the poet names as formative reading.
la.paulus_albarus.carmina: A medieval Latin collection of verse (541 lines, with no division into books) attributed to Paulus Albarus and assigned to the Carolingian era, its meter unspecified. The opening poem summons the nightingale (philomela) to surpass every human music — meter, organ, the Muses, and the lyre — and to raise its song in praise of Christ, while later passages bring in the cock (gallus) as a fellow and rival singer and frame the verses as 'responsa poetica' answering the birds. The collection thus recasts the classic nightingale topos in a Christian key, setting bird-song against lyric and hymnic praise. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact witness to the medieval transmission of the philomela and cock motifs, with diction inviting comparison across classical, biblical, and Carolingian song traditions.
la.petrus_of_pisa.carmina: A short Latin poem of 108 lines, of the Carolingian period and attributed to Petrus of Pisa, opening with a hymn to Christ as creator and redeemer who shattered Tartarus by treading down the dragon. The remainder praises a Paul addressed as the most learned of poets, comparing his command of Latin, Greek, and Hebrew studies with Homer, Virgil, Philo, Horace, and Tibullus, thanking him for instructing Frankish clerics in Greek grammar, and noting the imminent departure of a royal daughter who, with a Michael at her side, crosses the sea to grasp the sceptre of a kingdom. For readers hunting parallels, the poem offers a Carolingian example of hymnic Christian diction fused with courtly encomium, and of the classical canon marshalled as a pedigree for contemporary Greek learning.
la.petrus_riga.aurora: The Aurora is a medieval Latin versification of the Bible with continuous moral and allegorical exposition, transmitted under the name of Petrus Riga and presented here in P. E. Beichner's 1965 edition. Running to 16,762 lines in twenty-three books, it opens with prefatory verses in which an unnamed canon praises the book as manna from heaven, as Ezekiel's scroll written within and without, and as Moses' face unveiled at the light of Christ. The preface announces the poem's governing method, that the letter of scripture narrates the old law in figure while a mystical sense lies within its plain surface, pairing literal history with spiritual meaning throughout. A reader of intertexts will find a dense rehearsal of biblical diction and typology, verse after verse recasting the books of scripture into Latin poetry and cataloguing the allegorical readings on which later medieval writers drew.
la.phaedrus.fabulae_aesopiae: Phaedrus, a fabulist of the early imperial period, recasts Aesopic material in Latin verse, announcing in the prologue that he has polished Aesop's matter into senarii and that the book's double gift is laughter and prudent counsel for life. Its nearly two thousand lines consist of short animal fables, such as the wolf and the lamb, each rounded off with an explicit moral, alongside anecdotes in which fables intervene in political situations, notably Aesop speaking to Athenians groaning under Pisistratus. Satiric in temper, the collection repeatedly defends fiction as the veil behind which truths unwelcome to the powerful may be told. For readers of intertexts, it offers the principal Latin verse repository of fable plots, proverbial animal types, and sententious morals that echo through ancient and later literature.
la.plautus.casina: Casina, a Republican-era comedy in dramatic verse of some 961 lines, is printed here in F. Leo's edition of Plauti Comoediae (Berlin, Weidmann, 1895). Its prologue presents the play as Plautus's Latin reworking of an older Greek comedy, the Clerumenoe (in Latin, Sortientes, 'The Drawn Lots') of Diphilus, and appeals to spectators who savor veteran poets and old plays over the inferior novelties now current. The opening scene sets a household of an elderly husband, his son, and a long-serving slave, from which an intrigue of marriage and servitude unfolds. The explicit naming of the Greek model makes the play a prime witness for readers tracing how Roman comedy refashions New Comedy material.
la.plautus.mercator: A Latin comedy of the Roman Republic, the Mercator of Plautus is here printed from F. Leo's 1895 Berlin edition and runs to about 1,019 lines of dramatic verse. The prologue itself announces that the play adapts the Emporos of the Greek poet Philemon, and it is spoken not by a conventional expository figure but by the young lover, who catalogues at length the miseries and vices attendant on love before turning to his own case: dispatched by his father to the market at Rhodes, he has fallen for a woman of exceptional beauty. The comedy matters to readers of intertexts both as a Roman reworking of a named Greek original and as an early locus for conventions, above all the lover's catalogue of love's ills, that recur throughout later Latin and European literature.
la.plautus.trinummus: The Trinummus ('The Three Coins') is a Latin comedy of the Roman Republic by Plautus, composed in dramatic verse and running to about 1200 lines in F. Leo's 1895 edition. Its prologue, spoken by the allegorical figures Luxuria and Inopia, introduces a young man who has squandered his patrimony and announces that the play reworks Philemon's Greek Thensauros, with Plautus 'translating it into barbarous speech' and bestowing its Latin title. Readers of intertexts will find in it a central instance of the Roman palliata appropriating Greek New Comedy, along with the genre's moralising sententiae on friendship, wealth, and the chastising of erring friends, which invite comparison with both Greek originals and later Latin dramatic practice.
la.poeta_saxo.annales_de_gestis_karoli_magn: The Annales de Gestis Karoli Magni, attributed to a poet known as Poeta Saxo, is a Carolingian Latin epic in hexameters, preserved in five books totaling 2694 lines. It recounts the deeds of Charlemagne, opening with his sole rule after his brother Carlomann's death and turning early to the wars against the neighboring and still pagan Saxons, whose conquest the poet frames as divinely sanctioned. As a substantial verse treatment of recent Frankish history, it offers readers of intertexts a Carolingian fusion of classical epic diction with biblical and Christian material, and a point of contact for formulas shared with annalistic prose and panegyric tradition.
la.polignac.antilucretius: Polignac's Antilucretius is a Modern Latin philosophical work of nearly twelve thousand lines, conceived as a sustained rejoinder to Lucretius and the Epicurean school. Its opening invocation, addressed to a dedicatee named Quintus, declares war on the sect that abandons the world to fortune and denies providence and the life to come, calling instead upon the eternal Wisdom, Reason, and Light of God to guide the argument. Readers hunting intertexts will find the work in constant dialogue with De rerum natura, adopting Lucretian diction and opening formulas while reversing their doctrine in defense of a divinely ordered cosmos.
la.propertius.elegies: The Elegies of Propertius, an Augustan collection of love poetry composed in elegiac couplets, comprises four books totalling 3,982 lines. The opening poem announces the poet's capture by Cynthia and his conscription into a life of unrelenting passion, and the collection elaborates such elegiac staples as the lover's madness and servitude to Amor, mythological exempla like Milanion's labors for Atalanta, appeals to magic, and admonitions from friends. For readers hunting intertexts, the work offers the diction, situations, and mythological machinery of Roman love elegy in dense concentration, making it a rich source of verbal and thematic parallels within Augustan poetry.
la.seneca_the_elder.fragmenta: A short collection of fragments from the oratorical and rhetorical writings of the early Imperial rhetor Seneca the Elder, edited by Adolf Gottlieb Kiessling in the 1872 Teubner volume Oratorum et rhetorum sententiae divisiones colores. The excerpts survive as quotations in later authors, chiefly Quintilian and Donatus's Life of Virgil, and preserve a debate on tragic diction, specimens of bold declaimers' imagery from a controuersia in which a father kills his son and stepmother taken in adultery, an aphorism on oath-taking, and Julius Montanus's remark that he would steal verses from Virgil if he could also have his voice, mouth, and delivery. For readers of intertexts, the fragments are valuable because their phrases and anecdotes circulate within Quintilian and the Virgilian biographical tradition, so parallels may surface in those authors as well as in the declamatory corpus.
la.sigloardus_remensis.rhytmi: Rhytmi is a short work of 125 lines of Carolingian Latin verse attributed to Sigloardus Remensis, edited by P. v. Winterfeld in 1899. Its opening poem is a rhymed rhythmical lament for Bishop Fulco, praised as a wise, eloquent, and noble prelate who adorned the church and governed his people, before the poem recounts his treacherous murder by Guinemarus, who attacked him with sword, clubs, and armed soldiers, and closes with clergy and people bearing away the slain bishop's body amid curses on the murderer. Readers of intertexts will find here characteristic Carolingian formulas of episcopal encomium and invective, a vivid instance of the rhythmus as a vehicle for mourning a contemporary figure, and rich material for parallels in lament diction and the rhetoric of violent death.
la.smaragdus.carmen_in_psalterio: A brief Latin poem of twelve lines attributed to the Carolingian author Smaragdus, presented as a prologue to a treatment of the Psalter. Its speaker describes a copy of the Psalms enclosed in a golden and ivory case, outwardly plain yet bearing within the mystical words that David sang under the covering of the literal sense, and announces the aim of plucking choice gems from the book so that its pages may shine. The poem interests readers of intertexts for its programmatic contrast between the letter and the mystical meaning of the Psalms, its appeal to newer expositors who clarify the praise of the old prophets, and its reuse of stock prefatory imagery of the adorned codex familiar from other medieval verse prefaces.
la.smaragdus.carmina: A Carolingian Latin collection of roughly 500 lines attributed to Smaragdus, the Carmina open with a verse prologue that invites the reader into a libellus versifying scriptural matter: the deeds of the patriarchs and prophets, the Ten Commandments from Sinai, the Psalms, the three books of Solomon read as ethics, physics, and logic, and the preaching of the Gospels and apostles. The prologue's formula 'Scripturam retinet, grammatica redolet' announces poetry that retells the Bible while displaying the tools of the grammatical schoolroom, with classical terms such as Camena and the Cithaeronian plectrum alongside heavy biblical allusion. For readers of intertexts, the collection offers a compact witness to Carolingian biblical versification and to the fusion of scriptural allegory with inherited poetic diction in the medieval classroom tradition.
la.terence.heautontimorumenos: Terence's Heautontimorumenos ('The Self-Tormentor') is a Latin comedy of the Roman Republican period, preserved in some 1,112 lines of dramatic verse. Its opening prologue, delivered by an actor at the poet's request, defends Terence's habit of combining material from several Greek plays in single Latin works and explains why an old man has been given parts conventionally assigned to the young.
