The play's Greek title and its open engagement with Greek models make it a key witness to the adaptation of Greek comedy on the Roman stage, and a natural point of comparison for readers tracing such transpositions between traditions.
la.tertullian_pseudo.de_iona_propheta: A short Latin poem on the prophet Jonah, running to 105 lines, preserved under the name of Tertullian but of uncertain authorship and date within the later imperial period. It retells the biblical narrative from the destruction of Sodom through Jonah's commission to preach against Nineveh, his flight by ship from Joppa, and the storm raised in pursuit of him, framing the episode with reflections on divine patience and punishment. The verse recasts scriptural matter in classical poetic diction, with a storm description that draws on the idiom of Latin epic. For readers of intertexts it offers a specimen of biblical paraphrase in Latin verse and a point of contact between scriptural story and the inherited poetic tradition.
la.tertullian_pseudo.de_sodoma: De Sodoma is a short Latin work of later imperial date, some 167 lines long, transmitted under Tertullian's name and counted among the pseudo-Tertullian writings. It opens with the Flood and the covenant of the rainbow, then turns to the depravity of Sodom, the mission of two angelic visitors, and Lot's hospitable reception of them, retelling the Genesis narrative of divine judgment. Its blending of biblical matter with classical allusion — Scythian lands, Busiris, Antaeus, Circe — makes it a productive witness to how Christian Latin writers reworked pagan literary models. Readers hunting intertexts will find it valuable for parallels between Genesis traditions and classical epic diction.
la.vergil_pseudo.elegiae_in_maecenatem: The Elegiae in Maecenatem is a Latin elegiac lament for Maecenas transmitted under Vergil's name and consequently attributed to Pseudo-Vergil, assigned to the Augustan period. In its 178 lines the speaker, having lately bewailed a young man's fate in mournful song, now offers the aged Maecenas the carmina owed to a senior: the poem praises his Etruscan lineage, his watchful guardianship of Rome and of Caesar Augustus, his guileless simplicity against the jibe at his loose tunic, his devotion to Apollo and the Pierides, and his confidence that a slender book will outlast marble monuments, closing with the poet's resolve to stand as a faithful soldier of Augustus. For readers hunting parallels, it supplies Augustan elegiac diction dense with echoes of Vergil, Horace and Propertius, together with an ancient poetic memorial of Maecenas as friend, adviser and patron of letters.
la.vergil_pseudo.moretum: The Moretum is a short Latin poem of uncertain authorship, transmitted under Virgil's name and generally placed in the Augustan era. In 122 lines it follows the smallholder Simylus through a winter morning as he rises before dawn, grinds his meagre store of grain at the hand-mill, rouses his African serving-woman Scybale to kindle the fire, and finally prepares the cheese-and-herb relish that gives the poem its title. Its vivid attention to kitchen implements, food preparation, and the speech and bodies of the rural poor offers rich pickings for readers tracing verbal echoes of the Eclogues and Georgics and parallels in the ancient literature of rustic life.
la.walafrid_strabo.de_cultu_hortorum_carmen: De cultu hortorum ('On the cultivation of gardens'), a Latin poem of 444 lines attributed to the Carolingian author Walafrid Strabo, sets out in verse the planting and keeping of a kitchen garden. Its opening lines weigh horticulture among the quiet goods of life, survey the soils and situations that yield garden produce, and follow the gardener through the year's round, from winter's loosening grip to the spring clearing of a small plot choked with nettles. Written in a self-consciously classical idiom that invokes Priapus and adopts the georgic manner, the poem stands as a key witness to the survival of ancient didactic form and plant lore in Carolingian letters, and offers readers of intertexts a dense field of classical echoes reworked for a medieval setting.
la.walafrid_strabo.in_natalem_s_mammetis_hy: A Latin hymn of forty-eight lines for the feast of Saint Mammes, attributed to the Carolingian writer Walafrid Strabo. It praises the martyr's virtues and contempt for worldly wealth, recounts his endurance of adversity, his victory over princes and the dragon, and closes with a prayer for his intercession on behalf of suppliants. Readers of intertexts may find its dense hagiographic diction, including the coronation of witnesses and the conquest of the dragon, useful for tracing Carolingian devotional formulae and their parallels in liturgical poetry.
la.walahfrid_strabo.carmina: A Carolingian collection of Latin verse attributed to Walahfrid Strabo, comprising some 2,805 lines. The opening poem addresses a bishop as 'pontificum sublime caput' and exhorts him to build up the church's members through sound teaching and example, citing the Pauline injunction against giving scandal to Jew, gentile, or the church of God. The individual poems are of uncertain date within the Carolingian period, and no division into books is recorded. For readers hunting textual parallels, the collection repays attention to its fusion of direct scriptural quotation, episcopal admonition, and the Latinate school diction characteristic of Carolingian poetry.
la.walahfrid_strabo.carminum_appendix: A brief Carolingian Latin appendix of 142 lines of verse transmitted under the name of Walahfrid Strabo. Its opening piece is an epitaphic elegy mourning his death, recalling his crossing of the Loire and his burial at Auua, and addressing the passing traveller with the classic formula 'What you are, I once was; what I am now, you are soon to be.' The collection continues with verses in which the scribe Reginbert commits the completed book to safekeeping under a curse against unauthorised copying, followed by short complimentary couplets accompanying humble gifts. Readers tracing intertexts will find the epitaphic memento mori, the manuscript book-curse, and the conventions of poetic gift exchange present here in miniature.
la.wandalbert.de_creatione_mundi: De Creatione Mundi is a Latin poem of 285 lines on the creation of the world, attributed to the Carolingian poet Wandalbert. Its opening invokes the one and triune God as the eternal fount of goodness through whose Word the fabric of the universe was made, and moves from the creation and fall of the angels to the fashioning of the high heaven and the earth sunk in weight amid the great void. As a Carolingian verse rendering of the Genesis narrative, it invites comparison with other Latin creation poems and biblical paraphrases, making it a useful point of contact for readers tracing shared diction and motifs across the tradition.
la.wandalbert.horologium: The Horologium is a short Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Wandalbert, a versified lesson in reckoning the seasonal hours. Across its forty lines it pairs each month of the year with hours of corresponding length, notes the sixth hour as the one that keeps its own measure, and explains how shadows grow short in lands scorched by the south wind and long among peoples beneath the northern pole, framing its rule for a zone stretching from the Danube through Lugdunum and the Rhone to the Britons by the Ocean. As compact didactic verse on time-reckoning in the Carolingian manner, it offers useful parallels for the language of sun, months, hours, and the turning year elsewhere in classical and medieval poetry.

grc.septuaginta.genesis: The opening book of the Greek Pentateuch, translated from Hebrew in Alexandria in the third century BC and the oldest portion of the Septuagint. It runs from the creation of the world and the flood through the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to the story of Joseph and his brothers in Egypt. This Greek text is the version the New Testament writers quote when they invoke Adam, Abraham, or the promises made to the patriarchs.
grc.septuaginta.exodus: The second book of the Pentateuch, continuing the third-century BC Alexandrian translation of the Torah. It tells of the Israelites' bondage in Egypt, the plagues, the escape through the sea, and the giving of the law at Sinai, then turns to detailed instructions for building the tabernacle. Its Greek vocabulary for covenant, law, and sacrifice became the standard later drawn on by the New Testament and the early Christian writers.
grc.septuaginta.levitikon: The priestly law code at the center of the Pentateuch, covering sacrifice, ritual purity, the priesthood, and the annual festivals, including the Day of Atonement. It is organized as instructions delivered to Moses at Sinai rather than as narrative, and its vocabulary for sacrifice and purity later shaped Christian theological language. Traditionally ascribed to Moses, like the rest of the Pentateuch, and translated into Greek in the third century BC.
grc.septuaginta.arithmoi: The fourth book of the Pentateuch, named in Greek for the two censuses of the Israelite tribes that frame it. It narrates the forty years of wandering in the wilderness after Sinai, including the rebellion of Korah, the crisis at Kadesh, and the story of Balaam and his donkey, before ending with preparations to enter Canaan. Genealogical and legal material is interwoven with the narrative throughout.
grc.septuaginta.deuteronomion: The last book of the Pentateuch, presented as Moses's farewell speeches to Israel on the plains of Moab before his death. It restates the law given at Sinai, adds the Shema and other core declarations of Israelite faith, and closes with blessings, curses, and the account of Moses's death. Its Greek phrasing for exclusive devotion to God is quoted directly in the New Testament, including by Jesus in the temptation narrative.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_a: The first of the four Books of Kingdoms in the Septuagint, corresponding to 1 Samuel in the Hebrew Bible. It follows the judge and prophet Samuel, the rise and fall of King Saul, and the young David's anointing, his years as an outlaw, and his friendship with Saul's son Jonathan. The four Kingdoms books together form one continuous history running from Samuel through the fall of the two Israelite monarchies.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_b: The second Book of Kingdoms, corresponding to 2 Samuel, narrating David's reign after Saul's death: his consolidation of power, the bringing of the ark to Jerusalem, the dynastic promise delivered through the prophet Nathan, and the family disasters that follow his affair with Bathsheba and the death of Uriah, including Absalom's revolt. It continues directly from 1 Kingdoms, divided from it for length rather than content.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_g: The third Book of Kingdoms, corresponding to 1 Kings, opening with the succession struggle in David's final days and Solomon's accession. It covers Solomon's wisdom, wealth, and construction of the Jerusalem temple, the kingdom's split after his death into Israel and Judah, and the early kings of both, including the prophet Elijah's confrontations with King Ahab and Jezebel.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_d: The fourth and final Book of Kingdoms, corresponding to 2 Kings, continuing the parallel histories of Israel and Judah through the ministry of Elisha and other prophets. It narrates the Assyrian conquest of Israel in 722 BC, the reforms and failures of Judah's later kings, and ends with the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC.
grc.anthologia_graeca: The Palatine Anthology, some four thousand Greek epigrams by several hundred poets spanning the Hellenistic period to the Byzantine era, gathered by Constantinus Cephalas around 900 AD and preserved in a tenth-century manuscript rediscovered at Heidelberg in 1606. Its sixteen books cover epitaphs, dedications, erotic and convivial verse, and epideictic epigrams, and include celebrated short poems like Meleager's welcome to spring (9.363) that were widely read and imitated.
grc.aeschylus.agamemnon_hypothesis: The Agamemnon Hypothesis is a brief ancient argument, or prose summary, transmitted with Aeschylus' tragedy Agamemnon, the first play of the Oresteia, and printed in Herbert Weir Smyth's Loeb edition of 1926. In a handful of lines it recounts the plot — the beacon watched for at Clytemnestra's command, Agamemnon's return with Cassandra, her prophecy of her own death and of Orestes' future matricide, the killing of the king, and the rival claims of Clytemnestra and Aegisthus — and then appends the didascalic notice and a list of the dramatis personae. The didascalia places the production in the archonship of Philocles, second year of the 80th Olympiad (458 BC), with Xenocles of Aphidnae as choregus and Aeschylus placed first with the Agamemnon, Choephoroi, Eumenides, and the satyr play Proteus. Readers tracing parallels value the hypothesis for its ancient critical observations, including its praise of Cassandra's silent death and its remark on Aeschylus' distinctive handling of Agamemnon's murder, and for the performance data against which echoes of the play are commonly measured.
grc.aeschylus.persians_hypothesis: A brief Greek hypothesis, or prefatory notice, to Aeschylus' Persians, anonymous and of uncertain date, transmitted with the play. It reports the ancient claim preserved by Glaucus that the Persians was modeled on Phrynichus' Phoenissae, contrasts the openings and staging of the two dramas, and places the scene at the tomb of Darius with a chorus of elders in place of Phrynichus' eunuch messenger. It then summarizes the action of Xerxes' expedition against Greece, defeated by land at Plataea and by sea at Salamis, adds the didascalic note that Aeschylus won the tragic competition with Phineus, Persians, Glaucus Potnieus, and Prometheus, and closes by distinguishing Darius' ill-fated advance on Marathon from Xerxes' second invasion. Readers of intertexts will find it valuable chiefly for its ancient testimony to Aeschylus' debt to Phrynichus and for the didascalic information attached to the play.
grc.aeschylus.prometheus_bound: Prometheus Bound (Prometheus Desmotes), a Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, opens with Kratos, Bia, and Hephaestus chaining the titan Prometheus to a desolate crag in Scythia as punishment for stealing fire from the gods for mortal use. Across its 1,095 lines the chained Prometheus receives visits from the chorus of Oceanids, from Oceanus, Io, and Hermes, rehearses his civilising gifts to humankind, and refuses to reveal the secret foreknowledge that threatens Zeus's dominion. Its myth of Io, its catalogue of the arts Prometheus taught, and its language of tyranny, necessity, and prophetic resistance supplied later poets and prose writers with a rich store of mythic figures and memorable diction, making the drama a fruitful hunting ground for parallels and echoes in Greek literature and beyond.
grc.aeschylus.suppliant_women: The Suppliant Women (Hiketides) is a Greek tragedy of uncertain date by Aeschylus, preserved in some 1,072 lines in the edition of Herbert Weir Smyth. It opens as the Danaids, daughters of Danaus, land on the Argive coast after fleeing Egypt, invoking Zeus and recounting their descent from Io and their escape from a forced marriage with the sons of Aegyptus. The action centres on their ritual supplication of the king and people of Argos and on the city's deliberation over whether to grant them asylum. Its sustained supplication vocabulary, its handling of the Io myth, and its place in the Danaid legend make it a natural point of comparison for readers tracing asylum, marriage, and pursuit motifs in Greek poetry.
grc.anonymous.stadiasmus_magni_maris: The Stadiasmus Magni Maris is an anonymous Greek coastal sailing guide, of uncertain date, preserved in Karl Müller's Geographi graeci minores (Paris, 1855). Framed as a letter promising a learned correspondent the most accurate possible periplus of the great sea, its 358 lines record stade distances between successive ports, anchorages, headlands, islands, watering places, and cult sites, beginning at Alexandria and running through the Mediterranean coasts to the Pontus as far as Dioscurias, and onward to the Pillars of Heracles and Gades. Its dense toponymy, notices of harbours, temples, and oracles, and remarks on winds and sailing conditions make it a rich source of parallels for readers tracing place-name traditions, itineraries, and geographical formulae shared with other periploi, itineraries, and poetic accounts of the sea.
grc.apollonius_of_perga.conica: The Conica of Apollonius of Perga is a Greek geometrical treatise of uncertain date, edited by J. L. Heiberg in the second volume of his Teubner Apollonii Pergaei quae graece exstant (Leipzig, 1893). Composed in the proposition-and-proof manner of Euclidean mathematics, the portion preserved here establishes properties of tangents and secants drawn from external points to conic sections and circles, with particular attention to the hyperbola, its asymptotes, and its opposite branches, and repeatedly argues by reductio ad absurdum. For readers hunting intertexts, the excerpt offers dense examples of ancient technical mathematical diction — terms such as ἐφαπτομένη, ἀσύμπτωτος, and ἀντικείμεναι τομαί — and of ratio-based geometric argumentation later authors echo or reuse.
grc.archimedes.problema_bovinum: A short Greek epigram attributed to Archimedes, the Problema Bovinum challenges a 'stranger' to reckon the bulls and cows of Helios in four colours — white, dark, yellow and piebald — grazing in Sicily, and closes with added conditions on square and triangular totals that make the arithmetic famously demanding. The verse presents itself as a problem devised by Archimedes for the mathematicians working at Alexandria and sent in a letter to Eratosthenes of Cyrene, while a prose appendix recaps the solution in archaic numeral notation. Composed in Homericising hexameters, the poem reworks the cattle of the Sun familiar from the Odyssey as a computational exercise and stands as the outstanding instance of mathematics dressed in epic diction. Readers of intertexts will find here a nexus of learned epigram, verse epistle and number problem, bridging poetic form and Hellenistic geometrical enquiry.
grc.dionysius_calliphontis.dionysii_callipho: A brief prose periegesis of Greece, the Anagraphe tes Hellados ascribed to Dionysius son of Calliphon, an otherwise obscure figure of uncertain date, printed by Karl Müller in the first volume of the Geographi Graeci Minores (Didot, Paris, 1855). Addressed to one Theophrastus, it announces a swift, versified rendering of what older authors recorded and conducts a coastal circuit from Ambracia through Acarnania, Aetolia, Locris, Phocis, and Boeotia toward the Peloponnese, cataloguing cities, harbours, rivers, mountains, islands, and sanctuaries with mythological notices such as Agamemnon's foundation at Aulis and the oracle at Delphi. Its dense toponymy and cult legends make it a useful hunting ground for parallels with Homeric geography, the periploi, and later geographic literature. The corpus record preserves the whole as a single unnumbered line, with lacunae and a marked discontinuity in the sequence where the progression resumes at Crete.
grc.galen.de_comate_secundum_hippocratem: A short Greek treatise by Galen, De comate secundum Hippocratem asks what the name kōma signifies in Hippocrates: sleep itself, a sinking into sleep, or a drowsy drooping, as various earlier interpreters had proposed. Arguing chiefly from the Prognostics and the third book of the Epidemics, Galen contends that Hippocrates regularly opposes kōma to wakefulness rather than to sleep, distinguishing a sleepy kataphora proper to lethargic patients from a sleepless kind that can accompany phrenitis, before taking up the question whether such sufferers should be called phrenitic. For readers hunting textual parallels, the treatise matters as an ancient physician's exegesis of Hippocratic vocabulary, densely studded with verbatim quotation of the Epidemics' clinical case reports and of the Prognostic.
grc.galen.de_dignotione_ex_insomniis: De Dignotione ex Insomniis is a short Greek treatise by Galen, preserved in Kühn's edition of his Opera Omnia (Leipzig, 1823), which sets out how dreams may be read as signs of the body's underlying condition. Visions of fire, smoke, rain, snow and related imagery are interpreted as indications of excess yellow bile, black bile, phlegm and other humours, with the further proviso that timing, recent food and the dreamer's daily habits and worries must also be weighed. The discussion distinguishes such somatic dreams from prophetic ones, illustrating the difficulty of telling them apart with cases like the wrestler who dreamt he stood in a pool of blood and the man whose leg turned to stone and was subsequently paralysed, and it explains how the soul, penetrating the body's depths in sleep, registers its internal state. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact witness to ancient medical oneiromancy, in which dream imagery serves humoral diagnosis rather than divination.
grc.galen.de_ptisana: De Ptisana (On the Ptisan) is a brief Greek medical treatise by Galen on the preparation and therapeutic use of ptisan, the barley gruel prescribed for the sick. Opening with the complaint that physicians administer the drink without defining for whom it helps or harms, the work treats in turn the selection of water, the qualities of barley and its husks, the proper method of boiling, and the cooling, moistening, and cleansing powers that suit the ptisan to fever patients, with repeated appeal to Hippocratic authority. It then sets out the qualifications that must govern administration, including timing, dosage, and the disease states in which the drink proves dangerous rather than beneficial. Readers of intertexts will find it useful chiefly as a witness to Galen's engagement with Hippocratic dietary doctrine and to the technical vocabulary of ancient dietetics.
grc.galen.de_typis: A brief Greek medical treatise by the physician Galen, De Typis defines the typos of a disease as the ordered sequence of exacerbation and remission and surveys the periodic patterns of fevers. It distinguishes first and second, standing and moving, simple and compound types — quotidian, tertian, quartan, and semi-tertian fevers among them — and describes their symptoms, pulses, seasonal behaviour, and dangers, including differing ancient explanations of the semi-tertian's name, such as that of Agathinus. Quoting Hippocrates on the crisis of the tertian and appealing to what is handed down by him, the work offers a compact witness to Galen's engagement with the Hippocratic tradition. Readers of intertexts may value it as a source for the technical vocabulary of fever periodicity that recurs throughout ancient medical writing, edited in Kühn's Opera Omnia (Lipsiae, 1824).
grc.galen.quos_quibus_catharticis_medicament: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, edited in Kühn's Opera Omnia (Lipsiae, 1826) under the Latin title Quos quibus catharticis medicamentis et quando purgari oporteat — which patients are to be purged with which cathartic drugs, and when. Starting from the premise that purging healthy bodies is laborious and quickly exhausting, it sets out how to evacuate excess phlegmatic, bitter-bilious, melancholic, and serous humours in conditions such as gout, arthritis, apoplexy, epilepsy, melancholy, tertian fevers, and cancerous disorders, and how to prepare the body through rest, bland diet, and mild emetics before administering hellebore, colocynth, and related drugs, with attention to season, age, habit, the direction of evacuation, and the timing of doses in acute and chronic disease. Readers hunting parallels will find direct quotation of Hippocrates' Aphorisms, recurring humoural and pharmacological vocabulary, and first-person case histories of Galen's own patients that invite comparison with Hippocratic therapeutics and the rest of the Galenic corpus.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.catoptrica: The Catoptrica is a Greek treatise on mirrors attributed to Hero of Alexandria and of uncertain date, printed here from the Teubner edition of Schmidt and Nix (1900). Its opening argument holds that since nature does nothing in vain, reflection must occur at equal angles, so that the visual ray passing from the eye to the mirror and thence to the object seen follows the shortest path; the claim is then established by a geometrical proof employing congruent triangles. The corpus preserves the work only as a brief opening passage running to two long lines. Readers of intertexts will find here a compact ancient formulation of the law of equal angles and of the shortest-path principle, phrasings that circulated in later optical writing.
grc.herodianus.συμπόσιον: Συμπόσιον ('Symposium') is a very short compilation of etymological and lexicographical notes, of uncertain date and attributed to the grammarian Herodian, preserved as excerpts repeatedly introduced with the formula 'Herodian in the Symposium'. Its entries derive words for food, drink, and the symposium setting — such as βολβός, κάραβος, τάριχος, οἶνος, and ψωμοί — from supposed roots, and it quotes Homer and cites poets like Lycophron and Philoxenus in support. The piece offers readers of intertexts a witness to ancient etymological speculation and to the learned citation practices of the Greek grammatical corpus. It is edited by Augustus Lentz in Grammatici Graeci 3.1 (Leipzig: Teubner, 1867).
grc.herodotus.histories: The Histories of Herodotus of Halicarnassus, transmitted in nine books, announces at its outset the aim of preserving the great deeds of Greeks and barbarians from oblivion and of inquiring into the cause of their wars, opening with the rival Persian, Phoenician, and Greek accounts of the abductions of Io, Europa, Medea, and Helen. The narrative then moves through the Lydian story of Candaules, Gyges, and Croesus and onward to the rise of Persia and the conflict with the Greek world, interweaving ethnography, geography, genealogy, and embedded anecdotes. For readers hunting intertexts, the work is a central reservoir of mythic aetiologies, foreign logoi, and moralizing exempla whose phrasing and episodes recur throughout later Greek and Latin literature.
grc.hippocrates.jusjurandum: Known as the Hippocratic Oath, a short Greek prose pledge transmitted in the Hippocratic Corpus and attributed to Hippocrates, of uncertain date, in which a medical apprentice swears by Apollo, Asclepius, Hygieia, Panakeia, and all gods to honour his teacher, to share the art only with worthy sworn pupils, and to heal for the benefit of the sick according to his ability and judgement. The oath binds the swearer to abstain from lethal drugs and abortive pessaries, to enter patients' houses only for their good and free of wilful harm and sexual misconduct, and to keep silence about what is seen or heard in treatment that ought not be disclosed. Readers of intertexts value it as the most famous ethical document of the corpus, widely echoed, alluded to, and debated in later Greek medical writing and in the enduring tradition of medical oaths.
grc.homer.odyssey: The Odyssey is a Greek epic poem in dactylic hexameter, traditionally attributed to Homer and of uncertain date, edited here in Thomas W. Allen's Oxford text. Across twenty-four books it recounts Odysseus's homecoming from Troy, the wanderings he narrates in flashback among the Phaeacians, his return in disguise to Ithaca, and his revenge on the suitors of Penelope, framed by the maturing journey of his son Telemachus. Its motifs of nostos, wandering, disguise, hospitality, and recognition became models for Greek and Latin poets alike, and its phrasing and scenes recur throughout ancient literature, making it an essential point of comparison in the search for textual parallels.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_ephesios: The Epistle to the Ephesians is a Greek prose letter of the New Testament, attributed in its opening to the apostle Paul and addressed to 'the saints who are in Ephesus'; it is presented here in the SBL Greek New Testament edited by M. W. Holmes (2010). A product of the Imperial era, it opens with a great blessing over God's plan 'to sum up all things in Christ' and moves through teaching on salvation by grace, the reconciliation of Jews and Gentiles, and the church as the body of Christ, toward paraenesis on Christian conduct and spiritual warfare. Its elevated, liturgical diction and recurrent formulae — redemption, mystery, fullness, the heavenly places — echo throughout patristic and later Christian writing, making the letter a fertile source of verbal parallels for readers of intertexts.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannes: The Gospel of John, a prose book of the Novum Testamentum written in Imperial-era Greek, opens with the Prologue hymning the Logos who was with God in the beginning, became flesh, and brought grace and truth in place of the law given through Moses. The narrative then turns to the testimony and baptism of John the Baptist, who hails Jesus as the Lamb of God and the chosen one of God, and to the calling of the first disciples at the Jordan. Quoting Isaiah ('a voice crying in the wilderness') and retelling the ministry in spare, repetitive diction, the work constantly weaves scriptural allusion into its Greek. Its distinctive vocabulary of Logos, light and darkness, witness, and the only-begotten Son recurs throughout later Greek Christian writing and invites comparison with earlier Jewish, Stoic, and Platonic usage of the same terms.
grc.plato.symposium: Plato's Symposium, presented in John Burnet's Oxford Classical Text of 1903, is a dialogue in which Apollodorus recounts to Glaucon and other companions a banquet held at the house of the tragedian Agathon shortly after his first tragic victory, at which the guests each deliver a speech in praise of Eros. The sequence runs from Phaedrus, Pausanias, Eryximachus, Aristophanes, and Agathon to Socrates, whose account of Diotima's teaching on love is followed by the drunken arrival of Alcibiades and his eulogy of Socrates. For readers hunting intertexts, the work is densely allusive, quoting and reworking Homer's Iliad, Hesiod's Theogony, Parmenides, Euripides' Melanippe, and Aeschylus' treatment of Achilles and Patroclus, and its blend of comedy, myth, and dialectic has made it a recurrent source for later literature on love and desire.
grc.plato.theaetetus: Plato's Theaetetus is a philosophical dialogue in Attic Greek, framed by a conversation between Euclides and Terpsion at Megara, where the young mathematician Theaetetus is reported dying of wounds and dysentery after the battle of Corinth. The body of the work records Socrates, in the company of the geometer Theodorus of Cyrene, questioning Theaetetus on what knowledge is, testing and refuting in turn the definitions of knowledge as perception, true judgement, and true judgement with an account. Along the way the dialogue engages extensively with Protagoras and Heraclitean flux, supplies the image of Socrates as midwife, the wax tablet and the aviary, and a digression contrasting the philosophical with the political life, before closing in acknowledged perplexity. Its declared continuation in the Sophist, which resumes the inquiry into non-being, makes the pair a natural hunting ground for dialogue-to-dialogue intertexts.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_pericles_and_fabi: Plutarch's formal comparison (synkrisis) of Pericles and Fabius Maximus, written in Greek and preserved as the closing piece of the paired Lives in Plutarch's Lives (here in Perrin's edition), weighs the Athenian and the Roman statesman against each other point by point. It contrasts Pericles' command of a flourishing and audacious democracy with Fabius' guidance of Rome through the disasters of the Hannibalic War, and then measures the two men's generalship, foresight, treatment of political rivals, magnanimity with money, and public building. For readers of intertexts the comparison matters as a compact demonstration of Plutarch's comparative method and as a dense web of cross-references to episodes narrated in the two Lives, marshalling Greek and Roman exempla so that each illuminates the other.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_solon_and_publico: Plutarch's formal comparison (synkrisis) closing the paired Lives of Solon and Publicola weighs the Athenian lawgiver against the early Roman consul point by point. The passage assesses their lawgiving, their dealings with tyranny, their wealth and manner of death, and their military achievements, weaving in Solon's answer to Croesus about Tellus, his rejoinder to Mimnermus on the length of life, and the saying that he desired wealth but not unjustly gained. Since it quotes Solon's elegiac verses in Greek and sets Athenian and Roman institutions in direct parallel, it offers intertext readers a dense knot of Solonian quotation alongside Plutarch's method of measuring each statesman's fortune and virtue against the other's.
grc.pseudogalen.de_theriaca_ad_pamphilianum: A Greek treatise on the theriac antidote transmitted under Galen's name and printed among his works in Kühn's 1827 edition; its authorship and date are uncertain. Framed as an address to one Pamphilianus, the writer recalls what he saw and was taught in Rome and expounds the drug's virtues and proper use — against the bites of venomous creatures, against poisonings, and as a preventive taken monthly for long life and lasting health — with dosage rules and indications for fevers, coughs, dropsy, epilepsy, and other conditions, before setting out recipes for Hedyochrus's paste, for squill and theriac lozenges, and for the composite antidote that Andromachus called Galēnē and successors such as Criton renamed theriac. For readers of intertexts the work is valuable as a node in the theriac tradition running from Andromachus and Criton to Galen and the later medical compilers, since its ingredient lists, preparation instructions, and appeals to Hippocratic dietetics recur, with variations, throughout ancient pharmacological writing.
grc.septuaginta.odae: The Odae, or Odes, form a collection of biblical canticles transmitted as an appendix in manuscripts of the Septuagint and printed as such in Swete's Cambridge edition of the Greek Old Testament (1905). The songs are prose canticles in Septuagintal Greek attributed to biblical figures, opening with the Song of Moses at the Red Sea ('Let us sing to the Lord, for gloriously has he been glorified') and continuing with the song of Deuteronomy 32 and related pieces; the constituent songs belong to the Hellenistic-era Greek Bible, though the compilation itself is of uncertain date. Because these canticles circulated liturgically and supplied a shared stock of phrasing for Greek-speaking readers, their language echoes throughout later hymnody, prayer, and poetry, making the collection a rich source of parallels for hunters of intertexts.
grc.septuaginta.osee: The Osee of the Septuagint is the Greek version of the biblical book of Hosea, transmitted among the Hellenistic-era Greek scriptures and printed in Swete's Cambridge edition of 1905. The book collects the oracles of Hosea son of Beeri, set in the days of Ozias, Joatham, Achaz, and Hezekias of Judah and Jeroboam of Israel, opening with the prophet's marriage to Gomer and the symbolically named children through whom judgement upon Israel and eventual restoration are proclaimed. Its Greek diction, with phrases such as 'Not my people' and 'Not pitied', is the form in which Greek-speaking Jewish and Christian writers typically encountered the prophet, making the Septuagint wording a prime touchstone for tracing intertextual echo.
grc.septuaginta.psalmi: The Psalms (Psalmi) appear here in the Hellenistic Greek rendering of the Septuagint, as printed in Henry Barclay Swete's Cambridge edition of 1896. The book gathers the psalms of praise, lament, penitence, and royal acclamation that carry Davidic superscriptions in their Greek titles, along with liturgical rubrics such as the διάψαλμα, and opens with the beatitude on the man who meditates on the law day and night. Since its Septuagintal wording frequently departs from the Hebrew and became the scriptural diction most readily quoted and echoed by later Greek prose and poetry, the Psalter is a primary hunting ground for verbal parallels.
grc.sophocles.oedipus_tyrannus: A Greek tragedy by Sophocles, transmitted here in Sir Richard Jebb's annotated Cambridge edition of 1887. It opens with Thebes in the grip of pestilence, as suppliants gather at the altars and Oedipus, 'called glorious Oedipus by all', comes before the priest of Zeus; across its 1444 lines the king's inquiry into the murder of Laius turns upon his own parentage, ending in revelation and ruin. Its scenes of plague, investigation, and recognition have made it one of the most persistently echoed of Greek dramas and a rich source of parallels for later tragedy, poetry, and criticism.

it.dante.inferno: The first cantica of Dante's Commedia, thirty-four cantos in which the poet, lost in a dark wood in 1300, is led by Virgil down through the nine circles of Hell. Each circle punishes a class of sin by a penalty that mirrors it, and the damned tell their stories as the travellers descend to the frozen centre of the earth.
it.dante.purgatorio: The second cantica, thirty-three cantos on the mountain of Purgatory, where souls are cleansed of the seven capital vices on ascending terraces. Virgil guides Dante to the summit and the earthly paradise, where he departs and Beatrice takes his place.
it.dante.paradiso: The third cantica, thirty-three cantos ascending through the spheres of the heavens with Beatrice as guide, ending in the vision of God. Its subject matter is theology, light, and the limits of speech, and it repeatedly stages the poet's inability to report what he saw.

fro.chanson_de_roland: The oldest surviving French epic, about four thousand assonanced lines from the Oxford manuscript of the twelfth century. Roland, commanding Charlemagne's rearguard, is betrayed at Roncevaux and refuses to sound his horn for help until his men are lost, and the poem ends with Charlemagne's vengeance and the trial of the traitor Ganelon.

gmh.nibelungenlied: The Middle High German heroic epic of about 1200, in some 2,400 stanzas. Its first half tells of Siegfried's courtship of Kriemhild, his dragon-won invulnerability, and his murder by Hagen; its second half of Kriemhild's marriage to Etzel and the annihilation of the Burgundians at his court.

en.keats.ode_bards_of_passion: A forty-line lyric by John Keats, headed an ode and cast in brisk tetrameter couplets. The speaker salutes the 'Bards of Passion and of Mirth', who live double lives: souls left on earth endure in their songs, teaching mortals of sorrow, delight, glory and shame, while their heavenly counterparts keep festival amid Elysian lawns, Dian's fawns, and a nightingale that sings not a 'senseless, tranced thing' but 'divine melodious truth'. The closing lines repeat the opening address, rounding the poem into a refrain. Its double-soul conceit, its classical Elysian machinery, and its nightingale as emblem of poetic truth give it interest for readers tracing Keats's recurring images and the afterlife of classical Elysium in English verse.
en.milton.comus: A masque by Milton, running to 1,053 lines of blank verse, it opens with the prologue of the Attendant Spirit, who descends from the court of Jove to watch over the children of a noble Peer as they pass through a perilous, enchanted wood. The drama centres on their encounter with Comus, the sorcerer of the title, and on the reward that virtue wins after 'this mortal change' for its true servants. Dense with classical mythology — Neptune's allotment of the sea-girt isles, ambrosial weeds, the golden key that opens the palace of eternity — and steeped in the diction of the English masque tradition, the work offers rich material for readers tracing Miltonic echoes and the interplay of classical and Christian themes.
en.milton.paradise_lost: Paradise Lost is Milton's epic in blank verse, running to some 10,500 lines and divided into twelve books, which retells the biblical fall of humanity from the rebellion of Satan and his angels, through the war in heaven and the creation of the world, to the temptation and expulsion of Adam and Eve. Its opening invocation announces the design of justifying the ways of God to men, and the poem fuses Genesis with the conventions of classical epic — invocation, extended simile, and grand catalogue — while aiming at a scale 'unattempted yet in Prose or Rhime'. For readers of intertexts it is a central hub: it reworks Scripture, Homer, and Virgil, and its scenes, phrases, and characters echo throughout subsequent English poetry and prose.
en.milton.sonnets: A short collection of sonnets by John Milton, running to 128 lines and written in English and Italian. It opens with a nightingale sonnet that entwines bird lore, classical allusion and the twin claims of Love and the Muse, and then continues with Italian pieces in the Petrarchan manner, praising a beloved lady and playing on the poet's displacement from 'the fair Thames' to 'the fair Arno'. The bilingual imitation of Petrarchan diction and the dense classical and amorous allusions make the poems a productive source of parallels for readers tracing Milton's engagement with Italian and ancient verse traditions.
